speechtext: Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-unmarried man and woman registering as man and wife at hotel, etc.

I might also mention the case where a married man represents to a woman that he is unmarried and then marries her, committing bigamy. The woman who might be perfectly innocent would be liable under this section.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amendment suggested by the hon. member for Kingston and the suggestion of the hon. member for North Grey, have come to my attention only this afternoon. With regard to the latter suggestion, from the momentary consideration I have been able to give it, it might well be that innocent persons, man or woman, might be prosecuted if the innocent one was at the time under the belief that he or she was legally married. I think the suggestion is worthy of a few moments' consideration by the Committee. The latter remark applies also to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Kingston. The amendment, however, would be more easily accessible to abuse for the reason that it suggests no time over which the open living together as man and wife must have continued before it shall constitute relief from the penalties imposed by the Act.
I would like the members to express their views particularly on the amendment and on the suggestion of the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Middlebro).
By putting at the end of the section the words " knowing the same to be untrue ", it would improve the section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It will be necessary first to dispose of t'he amendment of the hon. member for Kingston.

I have no sympathy with, and I do not care to afford any protection to any man and woman who are living together in open adultery in this country. It may be permitted, but certainly it is in violation of everything we regard as good citizenship and good morals. Although perhaps we have not provided any direct law to punish it, we undoubtedly should not throw any protection around it". If any man and woman coming to Canada -have not yet been married, or have had no opportunity of being married, they can be married in Canada and should immediately comply with the law. I am not in sympathy with the amendment and do not think it should be accepted.

The matter is not as simple as the leader of the Opposition supposes. He says that people coming to Canada can be married. That is quite true, but people

may not be in a position to marry. I will mention an instance that came to my attention within the last month. A Canadian went overseas leaving in Canada a wife who went off with another man. The soldier foolishly paid attention to a girl in England, and she, believing him to be single, married him, not finding out that he was a married man until a child was about to be born. She came to Canada with him but the child was born prior to their arrival. That woman is in Canada living with the man in Kingston, wife number one not desiring to live with him. It is not a legal offence for these'two people to live together, and you cannot prosecute the man for bigamy because the offence was committed in England. Will it be contended that it should be an offence for this man and woman to register in a hotel as man and wife, notwithstanding the fact that they may legally live together in a private house? That would be an anomaly. I can give half a dozen instances of the same kind if necessary. I have no desire to throw protection around people of this class but I certainly think that we owe it to them not to set traps for them. That is the principle on which I advocate the amendment I propose. The endeavour apparently is to prevent a man and woman from going to a hotel and using it as a place of assignation, but it should not be held that a couple casually visiting a hotel should be treated as criminals simply, because they register or otherwise conduct themselves as man and wife when they are not such in fact. There are men and women living in this country as married people who are not legally divorced from their previous husbands or wives. How unreasonable it would be to say that they should live together in private residences unmolested, but that because perchance they come !to Ottawa to see the leader of the Opposition or go to Toronto to attend the opening of the legislature they should be made criminals if they register at a hotel.

I can only attempt to
argue this matter from the standpoint of common sense. It seems to me that the member for Kingston fails in his argument when he assumes that it is all right for these people to live together as long as they do not go to a hotel and register. I take the view that they are committing a moral offence, at all events, when they live together after discovering that they are not legally married. If they continue to live together they are committing an offence even if they do not go to a hotel
and register. The leader of the Opposition has expressed the case exactly when he says that the passing of this amendment will be equivalent to this House countenancing the living together of people who have no right to do so. To take the case mentioned by my hon. friend of the English girl marrying the soldier in good faith. What course should she take on ascertaining the facts? I think she should leave him at once, and the fact that she may decide to continue living with him does not excuse either of them if they gc to a hotel and register. There ought to be a law on the statute-books, if there is not, making it a criminal offence for people to live together who are not married.

I do not want the hon. member for Frontenac to put words into my mouth. Not for a moment did I suggest that it was all right for such people to live together. I was not discussing morals but law, and it is in that respect that my friend no doubt misunderstood me.
I said that adultery, at least in Ontario and Quebec, had never been recognized as a crime. The hon. member may be quite right in saying that it should be made a criminal offence, but if we are going to make it such let us do so in a direct way and not set traps for people. What I said was that so long as the law of Canada did not recognize adultery as a crime, I thought it was unreasonable that those who were living together openly as man and wife should be made criminals simply because they went to a hotel, lodging house, or boarding house and represented themselves as being married. I object to setting traps for people who are innocently-if I may use that word without giving offence to the hon. member for Frontenac-doing something they would have a right to do under the general law of the country but which becomes an offence when they register at a hotel or. boarding house, or represent themselves as having a certain status which they have not.
Is not this the same Bill that was before the House last year, passed the House, and was thrown out by the Sen^e?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the legislation in exactly the form in which it passed this House.

I have listened with a great deal of care to what the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) and the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) have said. I incline to the view expressed by the member



for Frontenac and also that expressed by the member for Cape Breton; I am very much afraid that if we amend this clause as the member for Kingston desires us to do it may be construed as giving the endorsement of this House to these irregular relations. Now, my hon. friend from Kingston seems to think that there is something unfair to the people living in these irregular relationships in this respect: That if they are living in a private house the law does not recognize their relationship as a crime, but if they go to an hotel or boarding-house and register there it is a crime. There is a distinction to be drawn. While these people are living in their own house they are not brought into contact with other persons so nearly and so intimately as they are if they register in an hotel or in a boarding-house.
Brought into the same contact?

Not into the same contact. Let us take the case of a summer boarding-house. Two people living in this irregular relationship go into this summer boarding-house. They register as man and wife, they are accepted as such, and they may become friendly with the people-many of whom will be young persons-in that hoarding-house. I think the situation is different when these people are living in their own house from what it is when they are living in a summer boarding-house, or any such establishment. I quite grant that it may be a little hard on such persons to be subject to this penalty if they go to an hotel; but after all, however we may sympathize with individual cases, or however we may in our own hearts condone their offence, nevertheless they have by their action prejudicially attacked the very basis of our society, and therefore I would think that the amendment of the member for Kingston cannot be accepted. I do not think we can accept it because.I am afraid it would give the country and the world in general an improper and false idea of the attitude of this House and of the people of Canada towards sexual relationships.

We have a moral law to observe in Canada as well as a criminal law. There may be sympathy coming to the man and woman who live as man and wife before they are married, but I have not heard any reason expressed for such sympathy. The most binding law which should be observed in the world to-day is a law not enacted by this Parliament. If there is no law on the Statute Book prohibiting one of the greatest crimes that is

taking place in this Dominion to-day, I think it is about time such a law was enacted. For my part I cannot let the opportunity pass without voicing my disapproval of it.

I would move that the following words be added at the end of the clause:
Knowing the same to he untrue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We must first dispose of the other amendment. Shall the amendment proposed by the hon- member for Kingston be adopted?
Might I ask that the amendment in question be read, as I was not in the Chamber when it was proposed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kingston moves to add at the end of clause 4, to form part thereof, the following words:
iNo persons who have been openly living together as husband and wife shall be prosecuted for an offence under this section.
Amendment negatived.

My reason for moving the amendment which I am about to submit is simply this: I think the Committee will agree that in most cases of bigamy, one of the parties is usually.innocent. Now under the clause as it stands to-day if, under those circumstances, a bigamous marriage was contracted, the innocent party would not only suffer from the results of that marriage, but would be liable as well to imprisonment. The operating words of the section are that either of the pa*ties "represents or pretends" that the man is the husband or the woman is the wife. What I say is that this should not be an offence unless the person who thus represents or pretends, knows that the statement is not true. Therefore, I would move to add to the end of the section, the amendment referred to. Then in a case of that kind the innocent party to the marriage contract would be protected.

I would agree with the hon. gentleman if his amendment did not impose on the prosecution the onus ~of proving a want of knowledge; I think the hon. gentleman will see the distinction there. I am not saying that his amendment does that, he has probably given more thought to the matter than I have, but if the onus of proving the want of knowledge does not rest on the person accused then we should be careful to see that it does. As my hon. friend knows, the onus must be somewhere. We want the onus placed

upon the right person, because it is very hard to prove that the party accused had such knowledge in a great many cases.
I would think that before any party is held to be guilty the proof of guilt must be forthcoming.

I am quite in sympathy with the amendment proposed by the member for Grey, but I do not think it is necessary. In order that a person be convicted under this section, the guilty knowledge would have to be established; there would have to be mens rea, and that being so, although I am absolutely in sympathy with the object of protecting an innocent party to these irregular alliances, I cannot see the necessity for the amendment.

I will submit this illustration to my hon. friend: An innocent woman accompanies a man to the hotel and the clerk asks: "Are you married"? and she replies, " Yes, I am married to this man here." In giving that statement she fully believes that she is married to him, yet under the section she would be guilty of an offence.
I do not think she would be liable, because she acted in good faith.
But the clause does not say that.
I submit wrongful intention would have to be established before the woman could be properly convicted under this section.
I would not want to take a chance on it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If I might present my own opinion, in a most humble way, it would be that the hon. member for Grey is right in his contention that that knowledge would not'require to be brought home unless the Act specifically called for such to be done. All that needs to be done to constitute an offence under the clause as it stands now is-we will take a single case -that a man by registering, or otherwise, represents that a woman to whom he is not married is his wife.
Now, all that has to be done is to so represent that a woman to whom he is not married is his wife; that itself the statute declares to be an offence. Consequently in my judgment-which I do not put forward as final by any means-unless we add " knowing the same to be untrue," this knowledge does not require to be brought home to the accused person.
138*
So far as the point raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is concerned, 1 would certainly be of the opinion without reserve, that if the law were to be amended merely as asked for by the hon. member for' Grey, then the guilty knowledge would require to be brought home to the accused by the prosecution, lit occurs to me- although I would like more time over these matters before discussing them that it would be better to state that the onus of proof of lack of knowledge should be on the-accused. And if the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) would so amend his amendment, then, subect to further discussion, I would be disposed to accept it.
Mr. JACOB'S: What is the law iii England with respect to 'these offences, particularly the offence under review?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as I know this does not constitute an offence in England.
Then why should we want to make it an offence in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We establish our own.
standard of morality-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -on the footing of our own conscience, instead of on the standard set by Great Britain.

The sources of our law
are from Great Britain; we follow her closely in the enactment of criminal law.
Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The principles of our
law, particularly of our constitutional law. we derive from -Great Britain; but our standard of morality we derive from our own conscience.

I am of the view.that this clause is liable to produce blackmail on an unprecedented scale. This legislation is hysterical. I think the -Criminal Code already sufficiently safeguards morality without the introduction of legislation of this kind.

I will withdraw my amendment and substitute therefor the following :
The onus of proof of the absence of knowledge shall be upon the person asserting the-same.

While you are perfecting the section, would it not be well to insert something in reference to cohabitation? The simple fact of a man passing off a lady as his wife in a hotel is not in itself a. crime.
^164
How are you going to prove cohabitation?

By their occupying the
same room. They do not generally do so except for an illicit purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid that if you put in the necessity of proving intention to cohabit you would only increase the difficulty of enforcing the law, and you would not absolve any deserving case.
Amendment carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section as amended carry?
Mr. Chairman, I move as an amendment that the clause be struck out of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's amendment is merely a negative. If he is opposed to the section as amended he Is at liberty to vote accordingly.

This Bill was before the House last year and was considered rather hastily I am afraid. In the Senate, where perhaps, if not wiser, there are older heads than in this House, they look at matters with that detached attitude which in questions of this kind is essential, they came to the conclusion that the entire Bill was useless, that it was provocative of blackmail and other offences of that nature, and consequently they failed to pass it. In view of that I do not consider it wise to send the Bill again to the Senate this year. 'This Bill was, as I understand, prepared and drafted by some association for the propagation of morality generally. It is not a request coming from any well recognized body, nor is public opinion, I venture to say, in favour of it. In view of all these '.circumstances I do not think it should form part of our law, particularly as we have, as I said before, a sufficient number of provisions of this kind in the Criminal Code to act as a drag-net for people desirous of committing offences against morality. As a matter of fact, I think we have too many of these measures already and they are not sufficiently carried out on account of that very reason perhaps. I am against the clause as amended and intend to so vote.
Section as amended carried.
Bill reported.

On motion of Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 88 (from the Senate) to amend the' Migratory Birds Con-
I-JIr. Devlin.]
vention Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 3-one-half fine to go to private prosecutor:
This provision is something that I am opposed to on general principles.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A treaty was entered into between United States and Canada for the protection of migratory birds. That treaty was ratified by Act of Parliament, and its provisions were embodied in the Migratory Birds Convention Act. The provinces, of course, had their own game laws, and, in the main, were enforcing them; but those provincial laws did not go far enough to ensure the protection of migratory birds. The subject matter having been dealt with by international treaty, the Dominion acquires jurisdiction; but the Dominion thought-and the migratory birds legislation is based entirely upon this hypothesis-that provincial legislation would be enacted to bring the laws in each province into conformity with the several provisions of the treaty and to provide for their enforcement. That hope has, to a large extent, been realized. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have brought their game laws into full conformity with the Migratory Birds Convention; British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec have brought their laws into substantial conformity-for all practical purposes, into full conformity -with the provisions of the convention and are in a reasonable manner carrying out those laws. But we have not been able to secure from the Maritime Provinces the legislation desired. New Brunswick, instead of bringing its legislation up to the requirements of the Migratory Birds Convention Act, has repealed its legislation altogether and throws the whole onus on the Dominion, very much to the disappointment of those who have at heart the enforcement of our migratory bird laws. Nova Scotia has not gone so far as that. Perhaps, in order to be accurate, I had better read just what has been done in this connection:
New Brunswick has not amended its game laws to comply with the treaty, but has repealed all its laws protecting migratory birds, on the ground that that is a duty now devolving on the Dominion.
Prince Edward Island has not amended its laws to comply with the treaty, and has no warden service.
Nova Scotia has amended its game laws, but it has omitted protection for wild beasts and ducks-except black, wood and eider-

an'd the open season for Wilson snipe and woodcock does not meet the conditions of the treaty. Moreover, Nova Sootia say they have not an adequate warden service to enforce the Act.
That being the condition of affairs in the Maritime Provinces, it becomes necessary for the Dominion, having regard to its obligations under the treaty, so to amend its Act as to enable it to enforce the law in those provinces. We must take power, therefore, to pass regulations covering minor matters of enforcement to enable us to carry out the law-it having been originally intended that these minor matters should be taken care of, as before, by the provincial authorities. That is the reason for paragraph (aa) in section 1, as to power of regulation under section 4 of the present Act. The same reasoning applies to the Bill throughout. Section 2 provides for penalties for violation and for the bringing of the goods seized to a justice of the peace who has power to order confiscation. The last clause, to which the leader of the Opposition advances his general objection, is also made necessary by the very same cause.
The laws of the various provinces which are now enforcing the Migratory Birds Convention Act, provide for the allocation of the fines. The provincial governments appoint wardens and game officers who a/re not under salary, but who are entitled, where they secure a conviction, to divide the fines, and in that way the enforcement of the law is secured. As, however, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island refuse to enforce the law-and this applies especially to Nova Scotia; the others refuse chiefly to pass laws-we must provide for some division of the fines as well, in order that a system of enforcement may be put into effect, without the necessity of our employing salaried officers for the purpose. That is the reason of this section. The hon. member will find that in his own province this very same law is in effect by provincial legislation. I read from section 108 of the Nova Scotia Game Act:
Every fine imposed and collected under the authority of this Act, shall be paid in full to the Chief Game Commissioner, who shall, except as elsewhere in this section provided, pay over the same to the Provincial Treasurer to be paid and applied to him as provided by section 104 of this Act.
(2)	When a complaint is laid and the information therefor furnished by a person other than a warden, the Chief Game Commissioner may pay one-half of the fine so collected to the complainant.
(3)	When the complaint is laid by a warden
under information therefor furnished by any other person, the Chief Game Commissioner may pay one-quarter of the fine so collected to such informant.	. i
So that the principle of the Nova Scotia' statute is merely being embodied in this. Bill to enable us to carry out the enforcement which apparently the province of Nova Scotia declines to carry out.

Has the matter been
one of negotiation with the members of the Nova 'Scotia Government? It is very undesirable to have any conflict, and I thought perhaps, that when some of the ministers were here lately, they might have had an opportunity of discussing the matter with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not conducted1
negotiations personally, but the Parks Branch has for many years been under the-charge of Mr. Harkin, and I know he has been conducting negotiations, although unsuccessfully, with those three provinces. I know Mr. Harken is very grievously disappointed that he is not able to secure that provincial conformity in the Maritime Provinces that has been secured in the others, and the consequent enforcement of the law.

Does this mean that
the Nova Scotia Government would regard this as a hostile measure, and that there would be a conflict between their laws and this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not want to speak too certainly on the point, but I rather think their attitude is this, that it is something of a burden and, inasmuch as we have made a convention, we should wholly bear that burden. I think I am safe in saying that they are quite in accord with the Migratory'Birds Convention itself.

The situation in Nova Scotia is that the administration of the Game-Laws is entrusted to an association called the Game Association, which comes, some-, times, to the legislature for amendments to the law. I do not know exactly what view they take, but I would be very much surprised if the Prime Minister of Nova Scotia and the other members of the Provincial Government would do anything that would' not be in harmony with the general law, and whatever is done is, I suppose, the finding of this Game Association, which collects those moneys, out of which they pay the game wardens in the different parts of the province. I would suggest to the minister that it would be well to endeavour to have no conflict as to the close season for game, wild and migratory birds. The close season is now. covered by the laws of the province of Nova Scotia.
[DOT]2166

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Undoubtedly, but we are bound in honour to live up to the terms of our convention, and as I stated to the hon. member, I am satisfied that the terms of that convention were satisfactory. Naturally inasmuch as the enforcement of them bears upon citizens of the- province, I presume the provincial authorities are not anxious to assume any greater share of that than they should. That is the general attitude. I realize there is no objection to this Bill; but if it passes, and if, hereafter, by the efforts of the hon. gentlemen or otherwise, the legislatures of the provinces can be induced to bring their laws into Conformity and to undertake the enforcement just as the other provinces are doing that will be much more satisfactory to the department and make a much better system all round.

I do not anticipate any trouble, unless it be on the matter of expense, concerning which all our Provincial Governments are sensitive. I know that this class of legislation has been regarded very favourably in Nova Scotia in days gone by, and I feel quite satisfied that if an effort is made the two Governments can be brought into harmony in the matter.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

Rumania is at war with Austria-Hungary at present and her credit may not be too good. Peace has not yet been signed and it is doubtful what countries will sign the treaty. I am opposed to the principle of lending the money of the people of Canada to the manufacturers of this country, for that is practically what this amounts to. There is an offer to Rumania, an offer to Serbia and I think to other countries to lend from $25,000,000 upwards, and the question arises in the first place as to the advisability of Canada going into the business of loaning money to the factories of this country to promote trade where they are not able to go out and get trade themselves. It is a fallacy to suppose that you can promote the trade of the country by furnishing credits to other countries to buy our goods. The trade of the country is done with trade; it is a trade arrangement. We are not going to sell Rumania rwheat, live stock, butter or eggs. We are not going to sell Rumania directly anything from the farm, but we are going to sell to that country manufactured goods; we are going to sell Serbia manufactured goods, and to any of the countries, apart from Great Britain, that get a loan from this Government will be sold manufactured goods. Great Britain can float a loan here at any timej and if Rumania wants a loan here she should be able to float one on whatever terms are possible.

But certainly she should not be able to come to the Government of Canada and float her debentures here .at par and take in exchange manufactured goods from this country. Canada to-day is indebted to Great Britain and to the United States. There is a heavy balance of trade against us, and we are in debt to various countries. Yet in the face of that we are going out to borrow more money from the Canadian people, or the British or American people to loan to another country. In other words, we are giving credit to doubtful customers at the expense of the people to whom we owe money to-day, with the result that we are only sinking deeper all the time. The manufacturers tell us they must have protection in order to cope in Canada with outside competition. Then they come back and tell us that they are not able to compete in the outside markets unless we supply them money to buy the goods. It can easily be seen where we are going to end if we attempt to furnish capital to the manufacturers to buy goods to ship out to all the [DOT] countries that are practically bankrupt in order to make trade for our factories. The argument was used, when the resolution upon which this Bill is based was before the House, that we must keep the factories going in order to create employment for labour. If the Government were to say: We will furnish this credit on the condition that all the profits that are made in these factories shall go to the employees and not to the manufacturers-then I would consider the proposal as being more sane and more justifiable. But to allow the owners of factories to fix their own prices for the goods, and their own price for labour, and then come to the Dominion Treasury for the money to carry that out, is, I think, a great mistake. If Rumania is not able to pay, what is the alternative? What are we going to do when this $25,000,000 becomes due? We must increase our taxation to pay the interest on that loan; and when our Western friends are asking for reductions in the tariff, or for the adoption of free trade, they will be met with the statement: Our responsibilities are so great that we cannot reduce or abandon the tariff. We are virtually bonusing these factories, causing a greater public debt, going out to incur what are practically certain losses that will entail increased taxation on our people. The Government is not only going to pay out this money to the manufacturers of Canada, but it is shovelling the money out to some foreign country; and the people of the Dominion 
will be called upon to pay. Should the loans not be liquidated, we will have to continue to pay the interest on these loans ourselves, and that will simply mean increasing the burden of taxation. I do not believe it is the duty of this Government to furnish any special industry or any special class of people with money to carry on business. If the Government has too much money on hand it would be better for it to purchase land from those who are keeping it out of use and sell it or give it to the returned soldiers, or to these factory employees, to build homes for themselves, rather than to hand it to some foreign country that in all probability will never be able to make repayment.
Mr. H. iH. STEVENS: The argument of my hon. friend is a most extraordinary one to my mind. He states that we owe Great Britain, the United States,- and other countries certain debts, and he deplores the fact. I wonder how in the name of common sense he expects this country is going to pay its indebtedness to Great Britain, or to any other country, except by the exportation of goods. Surely he must be aware that Rumania also owes Great Britain very large sums of money, if we send goods to Rumania and finance them in Canada we are simply going that far towards the liquidation of our debt to Great Britain. Being a man of very high intelligence the hon. gentleman must know that as a rule goods are not exactly paid for in cash to the country from which they are bought. It may be Spain, or Portugal, or France, or Great Britain, that is sending us goods; we also send goods to those countries; and the final outcome is a settlement by the process of exchange. He objects strongly to this Government establishing a credit for Rumania k* buy manufactured goods in Canada. If he is sincere he must just as strongly object to the Canadian Government establishing a credit for Great Britain or any other country-
Not Great Britain.

for the purchase of
other classes of goods. Of course I understand that my hon. friend will say, for the sake of his farmer constituents, that he does not object to financing the exportation of farm products, but he does object to-financing the exportation of manufactured goods. It is this everlasting baiting of the manufacturer, or other industrial person or company, that is causing sectional discord in Canada. This country is going to prosper, not merely by building up the agri-

cultural industry-which I am interested in and most anxious to see built up-but also by building up the manufacturing and the industrial interests. Canada does not possess merely agricultural resources; it has other immense resources-minerals, timber, oil, fish, and innumerable others; -and if we are going to liquidate the future debt of Canada it will be by the development of these resources and by encouraging the manufacturer. An ordinary business concern cannot ship goods to the centre of Europe with the expectation of securing an adjustment in the ordinary banking way. That is clearly impossible, and has been impossible for months and for years but through the agency of the British Government and through the medium of our own Government and the usual governmental channels and avenues, we are enabled to establish a credit for this country, and thus to send our goods out and secure payment to our manufacturers. This is not a bonus. My hon. friend is absolutely misleading and wrong when he tries to imply that we are giving a bonus to the manufacturers; we are simply establishing a credit to enable our trade to go on.
I think there is one principle that this House should get clearly into its mind, and get there just as quickly as possible, and it is this: If we are to meet in the next few years the enormous burden that Canada has incurred we must meet it through the process of foreign trade, through the exportation, not only of agricultural products, but of every class of goods manufactured from our natural resources. Unless we do seize upon that as an elementary principle in our economics, and bend every effort to direct the policy of Canada towards the development of our resources, I fear for the future of the country. I give the Acting Prime Minister and his colleagues the greatest credit for the courageous manner in which they are grappling with this problem, and providing for a medium of exchange, for a credit, for these foreign countries-especially for the enormous credits supplied by the Minister of Finance during the last four or five years for Great Britain, and for our Allies overseas, and I would say the more the Government can arrange these credits the better it will be for this country and the sooner we will certainly be able to liquidate our public debt, and relieve ourselves from some of the burdens which are bearing so heavily upon us.

It seems to me that the demand for such an enormous amount of money as will be raised under this legislation should not be submitted to the House at this particular juncture. In my opinion we are passing holus bolus a part of the Budget which is to be brought down some time during this month, if I mistake not, by the Minister of Finance.
We are anticipating and voting piecemeal what should be presented in bulk by the hon. gentlemen. If it were a small amount I would not object so much, because I understand there are pressing needs at times which require speedy and special legislation; but here my hon. friend demands that a sum not exceeding $350,000,000 be raised, and he is surprised perhaps that we offer some objection-not obstruction- to his large appetite for money. The preamble of the Bill does not in my judgment give a clear view of the situation. It seems to me an anomaly that on the very day the Peace Terms are announced to this House by the President of the Privy Council my hon. friend should preface his Bill with these words:
Whereas notwithstanding the armistice of the eleventh day of November last, and tjie extension thereof which has been granted by His Majesty and His Allies, has suspended the actual operations of the war between His Majesty and the German Emperor, the Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary, the Sultan of Turkey, and the King of the Bulgarians, it - is necessary that measures should continue to be taken for the common defence and security;
Shall my hon. friend for any longer period after the present eventful one come before Parliament and, always under the pretext of winning the war, ask for the speedy voting of such large sums of money?
I hope not,
My hon. friend enumerates in section 2 the purposes of this legislation. Among the purposes mentioned I find:	" (a) the defence and security of Canada." I am inclined to believe that this language does not convey quite the whole truth. The defence and security of Canada has never been so well provided for as at present. We have a laTge standing army, and our defence and security does not require, it seems to me, any large expenditure, if we have reached the millennium that has been sought for during so many centuries-that of permanent peace. The hon. Minister of Finance does not specify the amounts that are to be voted for each of the purposes enumerated, and consequently he does not say what amount out of this $350,000,000 will be applied to the defence and security of Canada.
Canada has during this great war done wonderfully well. She has raised, equipped and sent 500,000 men overseas, an array well

worthy of any great nation. But this was for the specific purpose of winning the war against autocracy. The nightmare is now over, the German Emperor and his allies have been thoroughly defeated. The people of this country made enormous sacrifices to maintain the honour and reputation of Canada. But, eager as they were to do their duty fearlessly and without questioning the heavy expenditure which was necessary, they are not in a mood-and I say it without any equivocation-to spend in the future, one quarter of the amount that has been spent annually during the last fateful four years. There is a general cry throughout the country that we should cut out the frills in the Department of Militia and Defence, that we should reduce mercilessly its expenditure and come back to normal. I hope that my statement will not be considered as anti-Canadian or anti-preparedness. I am simply voicing the feeling of the people in this matter. Before voting the amount asked for by this legislation, out of regard for the people and for Parliament, my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence should give us an outline of his peace-time policy. Hitherto all appropriations have been voted liberally and willingly in view of war times; but now we have reached peace times, and in this connection the Minister of Militia, in whose integrity and honesty of purpose I have the fullest confidence, should give to the country at the earliest moment his policy with regard to the organization of the defence and security of Canada during normal times.
With the second purpose of the Bill, "the conduct of naval and military operations in or beyond Canada and the demobilization of the Canadian forces," I am partly in agreement. Any money which is needed for the demobilization of our Canadian forces I am ready to grant immediately. But here again I require some assistance from both the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Naval Affairs. In mentioning the question of the defence and security of Canada in peace times, I had in mind our military organization on land-our military forces- But here reference is made to naval operations. I do not wish to re-open the naval debate, but might I not say here that the success attending the naval operations of Canada during this war-and those operations were successful, because our coasts were well guarded-was due entirely to the wise policy propounded by the late lamented leader of the Liberal party? Sir, what happened in 1911? The Liberal Gov-

ernment had passed legislation with a view to creating a naval force for Canada. That policy was combatted from two different angles. It was combatted in my own native province, because, forsooth, the defence of Canada by Canadian ships manned by Canadian officers and Canadian bluejackets was nothing less than suicidal. Canada, in the words of the opponents of that policy, was entering into the vortex of European militarism. That campaign carried some weight in the province from which I come. In Ontario the policy of a Canadian navy was combatted because, forsooth, it was too much of a Canadian policy and not sufficiently a British policy. 1 shall not refute both arguments at this moment, but I will say this: The Government that preceded this one came to office pledged at the first opportunity to remove from the Statute Book the blemish which the naval policy of the Liberal party was supposed to have placed upon it. But nothing of the kind was done- In 1914, when war was declared, the then Government was only too ready to use the much decried "tin-pot navy" of the Laurier Government, and Canada owes the protection of our coasts-of the Atlantic coast, at least-chiefly to the much abused Niobe and Rainbow. Subsequently the Naval Department, which had been organized under that policy, was reinforced and developed according to the provisions of that Naval Bill. It is a matter of pride for me, after so many years -eight years have elapsed since that campaign of 1911-to proclaim that, after all, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right when he propounded that policy-a policy which, we must not forget, had been approved by the Imperial Conference of 1911 and accepted by the British Admiralty.
Would the hon. gentleman object if it was proposed to lend the Niobe and the Rainbow to the British fleet?

There is a French proverb which my hon. friend may translate for himself: "A sotte question, point de reponse." We shall not be called upon to lend the Rainbow or the Niobe to the British Admiralty, which has been made much richer since the abject surrender of the German navy. But I should not be ashamed to lend to the British Admiralty, in case of emergency, the Canadian bluejackets and the Canadian officers who defended the coasts of Canada. The flag would be safe in their hands. I need not say, Sir, that I subscribe willingly and gracefully to a reasonable expenditure to

make permanent the Laurier naval policy which was so bitterly opposed in 1911 by some of the hon. gentlemen whom I see before me, but which, after all, has been adopted and will remain 'the permanent naval policy of Canada. But we are entitled to know from our great Canadian admiral, the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Ballantyne) his policy for peace times, as we should know from the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mew-burn)-two good Liberals, by the way, lost on the other side-
Major-General MEWBUBN: Lost, but not forgotten.

-his policy for our military forces on land during peace time. Am I asking too much from the Minister of Finance ('Sir Thomias White) ? Am I obstructing in asking that? I believe not. He is asking us, in anticipation of the Budget, to vote $350,000,000, are we not entitled to know the policy of Canada for normal times as regards our land anid naval forces? Clause (c) reads:
Purposes-the promoting of trade and industry and transportation facilities therefor.
I agree with the statement just made by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill).
I am not enamoured with this Rumanian venture, especially when I see that Rumanian bonds are being marketed from bucket shop to bucket shop and passing through the hands of Sir Clifford Sifton, who, by the way, has opened an office in the building rented by the Canadian Trade Mission in London. The Government. I think, should have prevented any such desecration of Rumanian bonds. 'If my hon. friend in asking us to vote money for . the promoting of trade and industry and transportation facilities, therefor is sincere and earnest, as he ought to be, I am in accord with him; but again I say if in those times of peace to which we are looking forward there is one Cabinet minister who ought to be in his seat, it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). During the last few years, we have been sadly missing the presence of a Minister of Trade and Commerce. Far be it from me to say one word against this right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster), in whose ability I believe and for whose splendid eloquence I have the utmost admiration. He has, I believe, been one of the best public servants of Canada; he is one of the Nestors of this House; but I am repeating only what I read every day in the Unionist
press when I say that as Minister of Trade and Commerce he has been a gre*t failure. He has not taken to heart his position as Minister of Trade and Commerce, a department which has been sadly lacking in force, ability and foresight to develop the trade of Canada. Canadians are often called " the lion's cubs." That means, I suppose, that we are the true sons of John Bull, who is the master merchant of the world, who for centuries has been sailing and trading on the seven seais of the globe. Not to speak of our high tariff, which is a barrier 9 p.m. to. our commerce, we have done nothing to even imitate from afar what has been done by John Bull and Uncle Sam. Long before the armistice was signed-and my authority is the London Economist and some financial reviews in England and the United States-^-England and the United States had their trade agents in all parts of the world. Any western member will tell us that in the far Canadian West, representatives of American firms have been trading with our Canadian farmers long before our own Canadian manufacturers. I have seen that stated in the press and I have heard it from the lips of' my hont friends who represent western constituencies. Therefore, anything which will tend to promote our trade and industry, I shall willingly grant to my hon. friend, but what does he intend to do? Has he given this Committee any explanations? Is he going to establish agencies and in what parts of the world? Is he going to create new avenues of trade and commerce? He does not say. What will our new tariff be?
We are at the present moment building a- fleet of steamers. Some months ago I was present at the launching of the Canadian Voyageur in Montreal, in my own constituency, at Vickers, and on that occasion I heard speeches delivered by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and some other prominent gentlemen from Montreal, and I read in the press that the Government had a very large programme of naval construction. But to my dismay, to my horror, I find that the ships we have been building in Canadian shipyards with Canadian material, are being used not for transportation facilities between Canadian and foreign ports, but by the wily Yankees between their ports and other foreign ports. This little item came to my hand the other day:
Barbados-Steamer Canadian Voyageur- Farr, J.-3,000 bags sugar.
That is the consignee.

St. {Lawrence Sugar Refining Co.-11,500 bags sugar.
Armstray, L. W. and P.-8,000 bags sugar.
This was carried from Barbados to New York. Now it is strange that our ships should not find any business for Canadian ports-Quebec, Montreal, Halifax, St. John, Three Rivers or even Toronto-in the exporting of Canadian produce. Have we built those steamers to send them to United States ports, to take on cargoes there for other foreign ports?

This particular sugar shipment came from Cuba, I think, and was consigned to the St. Lawrence Sugar Refinery. At the time the shipment was made the Voyageur could not get up the St. Lawrence, I understand, because the river was frozen.
What about Halifax, St. John, and Gaspe?
The railway rate would operate against those ports.

My hon. friend must
confess in all humility that the interests of Halifax were not well served.
No.

If my hon. friend had been Minister of Trade and Commerce, instead of being minister of all trades in the present Government, he would have seen that the Voyageur sailed from a Canadian port to a foreign port. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, and I am in earnest, we have done practically nothing. I know, of course, that our export trade during the war has wonderfully increased, but this was due to our war industries, and there is an end to those industries. To-day we must revert to peace trade and peace activities, and long before peace was declared an anny of commercial agents from England and the United States were marching through many countries in order to capture as much as possible of their trade. I am told that Mr. Hoover himself, although his mission was to feed the Central Empires, has captured the blue ribbon for the United States, having secured enormous orders for American concerns. But Canada has done nothing at all.
How did he do it? By advancing them money?

I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance either to secure a good sinecure for the present incumbent of the Department of Trade and Commerce -I want the best for Sir George Foster,
(Mr. Lemieux.]
because he deserves it-or to promote him tp some other department and appoint in his stead some "live wire" so that Canada shall secure some of the world's trade in the coming peace times.
I said a moment ago that this legislation is a camdufiaged Budget, and it is. In connection with this third purpose "the promoting of trade and industry, and transportation facilities therefor" the Minister of Finance owes the country an outline of the fiscal policy of the Government. Does he believe that trade and commerce and industry can be promoted if the country is kept in ignorance of the tariff changes that are to be made? Surely not. My hon. friend must know the sentiment of his followers. To use a somewhat vulgar expression, which is nevertheless in common parlance, he is between the devil and the deep sea-between the high protectionists on the one hand and the free traders of his party on the other-and he is simply marking time, awaiting the return of the Prime Minister or some heavenly inspiration. I am afraid, however, that his inspiration will come from the opposite direction-
The fourth purpose is this: "The carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the Governor in Council in consequence of the war." Mr. Chairman, I am afraid of that purpose. I am not timid; I have some courage left in my bones, but I must confess I am really in dread of that fourth purpose. What are those measures that are deemed necessary? What are those vague measures that are deemed advisable? Should not those measures be made known to Parliament, and not left to the sweet will of the Governor in Council? Already the practice of governing by Order in Council has been too much abused, and I am really in dread of what may happen when my hon. friend is granted the powers he is seeking under this fourth purpose.
The fifth purpose is this:	"Payments
made on expenditure incurred during the fiscal year ending the thirty-first day of March, nineteen hundred and nineteen, for the purposes mentioned in the War Appropriation Act, 1918, and in excess of the amount authorized by the said Act." It is true that my hon- friend gave the House the other day row after row of figures running into the millions-indeed into the hundreds of millions of dollars. We must face the situation; the millions are there. As Mt. Thiers, the liberator of the French territory, once said, referring in the House of Representatives in France to the inevi-

table expenditure of several millions: "Sa-luez, Messieurs, vous ne les reverrez plus." After having seen my hon. friend marshalling his long array of millions the other diay I also am inclined to repeat with Thiers, "Hats off, gentlemen; you shall never see those millions again." To be serious, I think my hon. friend should take us into his confidence a little more. Assuredly, I am not asking him to give us the inner secrets of his soul; I am not asking him to unbosom before this House, because it would be a terrible confession and I am afraid there would be no absolution for the many crimes he is guiilty of. But at least he should pay the taxpayers of Canada the compliment of telling them why this enormous sum of money is needed, and to w'hat specific purposes it is to be applied. I am afraid of being accused by my hon. friend of obstruction. I will say no more, but I again appeal to him to be a little clearer as to numbers 3 and 4, and to my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and also the Minister of Naval Affairs I would suggest that we might have an outline for the benefit of the country of their respective policies.
Major-General MEWBURN: I have listened with considerable interest to the hon. gentleman's eloquence, but I am at a loss to understand several of the statements he has made. If he will turn to Hansard of April 29th, when I had my main estimates for the Militia Department before the Committee, he will see that he was very complimentary to me on that occasion when I attempted to give a brief resume of the future policy of the militia forces -of Canada. The portion of the Bill now before the Committee does not include one item for the upkeep of the military forces of Canada after demobilization. My hon. friend will see that on page 1404 of unrevised Hansard, April 10, the Acting Prime Minister gave complete details of expenditure, particularly of the militia forces of Canada in connection with this Bill. I am sure my hon. friend is as anxious now, as he always has been, to assist in every way the prosecution of the war by paying for our soldiers overseas. I do not believe for a moment that he means now to leave those soldiers alone and not consider the complete demobilization of the troops. Every dollar of this expenditure is simply to pay the allowances of soldiers on active -service to-day, including war service gratuity; deferred pay, which amounts to some $36,000,000, which is money belonging to the troops, held back in the w'is-dom of the Government, and now being paid them on discharge, plus
interest; also assigned pay some $11,000,000; separation allowance to dependents of the troops; and subsequent items including transportation and feeding of troops until complete demobilization. Therefore, no portion of the money included in this Bill is to be utilized for the upkeep of military forces beyond the period of complete demobilization, which I am just as anxious as any one else to see carried out as early as possible.
Regarding the future policy as far as the militia is concerned. I regret that my colleague the Admiral of the Fleet (Mr. Ballantyne) is not here to give an account of the Navy, but I explained the other night as to the future policy of the military forces, that, after very careful consideration, we appointed an inter-departmental committee to consider ways and means for reorganization. The Chairman of the Committee is General Otter, who has had a very large experience in the militia of Canada; and it is also proposed to have an officer who has had distinguished service at the front-, one from the permanent force, one from the active militia, and one who has never been associated with the militia until this war. The Committee are to visit the various military districts, to consider ways and means and probably at another session of the House to bring in some concrete proposal as to how far the militia should go. The duty of the committee is to consider and report how best to give effect to the proposal that with a view to preserving their traditions and identities, the several units of the C. E. P. which have served at the front should be incorporated in the Canadian Militia-this without avoidable increase of establishments, without prejudice to the divisional system of organization, and with due regard to the services which at various times, both before and during the war, the militia itself has rendered. That is practically the substance of tlie duties of the committee. The present idea is to endeavour to rehabilitate the militia units as well as possible. The permanent corps had a strength prior to the war of 3,000, kept up during the war for service overseas by reinforcements. Those men who come back are entitled to discharge or to go on pension. It is proposed to increase that permanent force as a temporary measure to 5,000 men throughout Canada. That will be practically all the force in Canada, and will be held in aid of the civil power if necessary. At the present time it is not proposed to train the militia which is in a disorganized state. Possibly it may

be considered necessary to train a portion of the militia next fall, but no definite policy has been arrived at and il think it would be premature for us to lay down a concrete military policy just at present.

My hon. friend must
have in- mind the very large reduction in the expenditure of the Militia 'Department for peace time. Can he state what he thinks approximately will be required in the future for the appropriations of the Militia Department? What amount does he expect to apply as appropriations for the Department of Militia and Defence in the future?
Major-General MEWlBURN:	I should
say approximately from four to seven million dollars.

I wanted to know what was in my hon. friend's mind for the future in peace time. It is a relief to hear that he intends to live up to $4,000,000, but he will have to cut many frills.
Major-General MEWBURN:	At present
the problem of demobilization, not only bringing troops back, but clearing up all records, documents, etc., is an enormous one.
For instance, at the present time some one hundred and seventy thousand ledger sheets have been returned from overseas within the last few weeks-that is, ledger sheets of the individual troops that are *coming over as the men are demobilized. The work of checking and dealing with every individual man's' account is enormous. In addition, there are some five hundred tons of files being gradually returned from overseas to the Militia Departr ment here. That includes all the records *and documents that have been moved from General Headquarters in France back to JSngland, and the records and documents from the various Record Offices in England. It takes an enormous amount of labour and some staff to complete and get all these documents into shape. Furthermore, there is the file containing documents of every individual man with the Canadian Expeditionary Force, amounting in all to over six hundred thousand files. These documents, containing the medical history of every man, it is most essential should be carefully kept so as to protect this country in the matter of claims for pensions in the future. The Pension Department requires these files, also the Department of 'Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment-when the men are discharged, which work has nothing to do with [Major-General Mewbum.]
the Militia Department-and the Land Settlement Board in connection with soldiers' settlement. Then there is the large problem of hospitalization. We are taking care of the returned soldiers-officers, noncommissioned officers, and men-in the various hospitals throughout Canada, and we estimate that by next February we should be through with the military hospitalization, but that is only an estimate. In November, 1918, the casualties of Canadian corps were something like 45,000. The difficult problem was to estimate the number of casualties or invalids coming back to Canada. We estimated, as well as we could, on information from the medical service, that somewhere about May there would be approximately 18,000 invalids still coming back from overseas. I am glad to say that we were generous on our estimate; that the patients in the military hospitals in England are being evacuated a little quicker than we expected and becoming convalescent cases. The last figures from France, I think, showed that there were about seventeen hundred still to be evacuated from that country. The total number of patients in England and France up to a week ago was slightly under 14,000, but many of these-

How many are there in Canada?
Major-General MEWBURN: In the various hospitals in Canada close on to 14,000. A very large number of those men, if they do not require any further treatment in the military medical hospitals, will be discharged, and will come under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment for vocational training, and so on. Referring to, the amount that is required out of this particular vote, it is purely and simply to complete the pay and allowances, and deferred pay and war gratuity for the troops that are on active service. We estimate that ff we have no setbacks, our troops will be brought back from overseas by August. I believe we shall enter upon next year with a very small staff both at Headquarters and in the military districts. I am quite satisfied of that. I think if my hon. friend would' look at these items on the page referred to, he will see that they have nothing

to do with the future upkeep of the militisl and are not intended for military purposes in Canada beyond actual necessary cleaning-up purposes.

, Major-General MEWBURN:	Only to
that.

While we are upon this
subject, I would like to draw the minister's attention to a phase of military life which has been brought out in a letter received by me to-day from a soldier's father. Speaking in regard to his son, the writer says:
He enlisted at London, Ontario, in December 1915, went to England in January 1916, and to Prance in June 1916, and has been there on active service ever since, while his wife and child are with us. The Canadian Authorities in Division One, London, Ont., took the initiative in the signing up of the boys conducting their medical examination, etc. They advised them to enlist in the Imperial Mechanical Transport, as the C.E.F. at that time did not need any more recruits. They took their advice. Had my son signed up with the C.E.F., he on discharge would have been entitled to $100 per month for six months, a total of $600. Instead of that the B.E.F. will only grant $75 all told, a difference of $525.
Now since this Bill, as it is worded, refers purely to the demobilization of Canadian soldiers, I thought it would be an opportune time to ask the minister whether he intends in the expenditure of these moneys to provide to the extent of $525 for the war gratuity of a young Canadian soldier who is married and has a wife and child? If the minister intends to do nothing in that direction, will he make representations, if such may be proper, to the Imperial authorities to influence them to act equitably to this young man who was misled, according tQ my information, by the officers of the minister's department 'at London. On inquiry, I find that there are overseas many hundreds of Canadian young men who have gone to the front in some capacity or other, having either transferred to, or enlisted directly in this country in, the Imperial Forces. If the Imperial Government are doing nothing for these young men, I want the minister to tell me whether he intends to do anything for them, and whether this fund will be available for that purpose? If the minister replies in the negative, I would say that I would be rather ashamed to live in the country if such inequity should be passed out to these young men who fought for their King and country as Canadians
in the Imperial Army. I take this opportunity of asking the minister whether he has considered the matter, and if he has not done so, to state, if he can, that he will consider it and that he will look favourably upon the application which I am making on behalf of these men.
Major-General MEWBURN: The subject which the hon. member has raised has certainly been given a good deal of consideration, particularly of late. The war gratuity does not apply to such a man as the hon. gentleman has referred to, hut I may say that some little time ago suggestions and claims came from different soldiers regarding the war gratuity, a few of the class are Imperial army reservists, who, when the war began, left Canada and rejoined their units. The claim has been made that those men should participate in this war gratuity, or be paid the difference between what they received from the Imperial Government and what Canada is giving. There were also pensioners resident in Canada who returned to England and re-enlisted-I am speaking of British pensioners, on whose behalf application was made; likewise, men who especially enlisted in Canada in the British Army Service Corps and the Royal Engineers ; men who enlisted in Canada and the United States (British subjects), and Canadians who enlisted while overseas in the Imperial Forces.
I may say for the information of my hon. friend that a committee has been working on this for the last week, and while it is not a Committee of the House, I understand, unofficially, that several hon. members who have had those matters brought before them have been meeting and are drafting a memorandum, which I believe they are giving to the Government, and I know it includes such items as those. Whether the Government can see their way to concede those or some other items, I am not prepared to say. But there are a great many hardships. A great many Canadians I know joined the Imperials, and a'large number of university graduates went over to England and took commissions. I understand the Imperial Government are giving very much larger gratuities to officers than the Canadian Government, but not anything like what we are giving to the rank and file. But that matter is having our most serious consideration.

I am very pleased indeed with the explanation given by the Minister of Militia as to what he intends to do regarding militia matters, and it is interesting to know that he has already appointed a committee of eminent soldiers who during the next twelve months will visit the different militia districts and get information to enable him to lay a concrete proposition before the House next session. I understood from his remarks that these three gentlemen are military men. I have no objection to their appointment, but I would suggest for his consideration that he also appoint to that committee at least one business man. It seems to me that the matter should not be left entirely in the hands of men who have served in the army or who are officers of the Militia Department.
Dealing with section 2 of this Bill, I see that a part of the $350,000,000 to be borrowed is to be spent (a) for the defence and security of Canada; and (b) for the conduct of naval and military operations in or be-jond Canada and the demobilization of the Canadian forces. I do not think it is necessary to spend much time in discussing subsection (a), because the Minister of Militia, when his Estimates were being discussed recently, convinced me that it is not his intention to spend any money in the defence and security of Canada except what is absolutely necessary to continue the staff at headquarters and to provide for the upkeep of other pre-war military organizations in different parts of the country.
With regard to subsection (b), I am in hearty agreement with that portion which states that this money is to be spent for "the demobilization of the Canadian forces." I think we all agree that every effort should be made to have our Canadian boys returned from France and England at the earliest possible moment, so they may be discharged and take their place again in civil life. But with the first part of this

subsection "for the conduct of naval and military .operations in or beyond Canada,"
I am not in agreement- I do not think it is necessary to provide that one dollar should be expended in military operations during' the year 1919, except as outlined by the Minister of Militia. Instead of spending money on military operations, we should strain every nerve to cut our expenditures down to the very lowest possible minimum. Let us see what we have spent for this purpose in the last four years. In 1914-15, the first year of the war, we spent $53,176,613.55; in 1915-16,	$160,433,416.42;
1916-17,	$298,291,030.66;	1917-18,	$316,669,-
871.95, and in 1918-19 to March 31, $289,229,119.38, making a total expenditure of $1,117,791,051-96 to equip and send our boys overseas and maintain them there. In addition there was spent on account of mUi-tary hospitals about $12,800,000, and with cur other expenditures in connection witn the war we spent up to March 31 of this year a total sum of $1,225,114,112.36. A great deal of criticism has been directed against the extravagant expenditure of part of this money, but so far as the Department of Militia and Defence is concerned, we have the satisfaction of knowing that while they have spent an enormous amount of money, and in some cases have spent it not as wisely as we would like to have it spent, yet they despatched at least 500,000 men overseas to fight for the Empire, and Canada to-day realizes that the splendid valour =hown by our soldiers on the battlefields of Flanders and Belgium fully justifies the action of the Department of Militia and Defence. 'Consequently, while as I said before there may be some criticism of the-manner in which portions of this large amount of money were spent, yet Canadians everywhere feel that they have received value in return for what has been disbursed.
What about the Naval Department? My good friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) thinks that the naval defence of Canada is a great deal better than it really is. Perhaps the reason for that is that "distance lends enchantment to the view," and my hon. friend, living as he does in Ottawa, does not know a great deal about naval defence on either the Atlantic or the Pacific coast. Since 1914 the enormous sum of $30,982,683.22 has been spent by the Naval Department on what is termed "strictly war expenditure;" and in addition millions of dollars have been expended in keeping up the dockyards and naval colleges at Halifax and Esqui-malt and in paying the salaries of officials

at Ottawa, Halifax and other places. Speaking for the moment of what is termed " strictly war expenditure," in 1914-15, $3,096,125.35 was expended; in 1915-16, $3,274,019.94; in 1916-17, $3,806,329.19; in 1917-18, $9,666,229.14; and in 1918-19 to March 31, $11,139,979.60; making, as I said before, a grand total of $30,982,683.22 I am going to show, Mr. Chairman, that [DOT]this $31,000,000 was practically all wasted, that it was not spent in the interest of the taxpayers of Canada; that it was entirely unnecessary, and did not in any particular, or in any way help to defend Canada or to protect the property of her citizens.
Before trying to show the Committee exactly what has happened during the war, I think it would be well for a few moments to give the history of naval matters in Canada. In giving this short resume of naval history, I do not intend to deal with the matter from a political standpoint In 1909 Sir George Foster introduced into the House of Commons a resolution, the substance of which was that Canada should proceed with the building of a Canadian navy for the protection of our own coasts. This resolution, with a slight amendment made by the leader of the Government, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was adopted by the whole House, the members being unanimous in their decision that this was the proper course to pursue. In 1911 the Government called for tenders for the construction of cruisers of the Bristol type, and at the time they went out of power in 1911 tenders had been received from a firm in Canada which was willing to build these ships. No action was taken on these tenders by the incoming Government, and the whole matter was dropped for a year or two until Sir Robert Borden introduced a resolution to pay to Britain $35,000,000 to purchase three dreadnoughts, and, in a speech delivered by him, abandoned the Canadian navy. Some of the arguments which were used by Sir Robert Borden were that it would take fifty years for Canadian workmen to leam how to build these ships, and that we could not supply riveters. In view of the fact that for the last few years Canadian workmen have been turning out steel ships in different shipyards in Canada, the argument is refuted that -we could neither build the ships nor provide the riveters. Most of the work which has been done in the last few years by Canadian workmen is second to none and will pass inspection by either Lloyds or the American Bureau of Shipping.
At the same time it will be remembered that Mr. Winston Churchill informed us 139
that there was no land in Canada suitable for building these ships, a statement which at the time was laughed to scorn by every person but those who wished to damn the idea of a Canadian navy.
The Senate of Canada refused to sustain the vote of the House of Commons, and consequently the $35,000,000 never reached England, and the whole matter of a Canadian navy or of a contribution to the British navy died a natural death.
It is true that at this time we had at Halifax the Niobe and at Esquimalt the Rainbow, two cruisers which had been purchased by the Liberal Government. Up to 1911 the crews of these ships had been kept at full strength and had been used for training purposes so that young Canadians could take courses in naval instruction. Shortly after Hon. J. D. Hazen assumed the position of Minister of Naval Affairs the crews of these ships were disbanded, the boys sent home and only a few men kept on board to act as caretakers. It is just as well-perhaps, though it is not as well- that the gentleman who was then Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not here to-night to answer what I have to say. I may add that I do not lay any blame at the door of the hon. gentleman who to-day has charge of the Department of Naval Affairs (Hon. Mr. Ballantyne), because at the time he took charge, matters were in such a condition that it was impossible to remedy them. It is well, perhaps, that the gentleman who was in charge of naval affairs at that time now has a good, soft position in New Brunswick. A black eye was given the Canadian navy when the action of the then Minister of Naval Affairs showed that he was not in sympathy with any Canadian naval movement. Consequently, when the war broke out, the Niobe was not in fit condition to help protect the coast of Nova Scotia. Although immediately upon war being declared, orders were sent to Halifax to prepare the Niobe for sea and a part crew was sent from Esquimalt to man her, it was found that her boilers were in such condition that it would take several months to put her in a seaworthy condition. I make the statement here that if the Niobe had been ready to proceed to sea the morning that war was declared she would have succeeded in capturing prizes which would have p.aid the Canadian expenditure for war purposes during the first year of the war.
It was certainly humiliating for Canadians at Halifax to see this ship tied to her dock, grounded on her beef bones, weeks and weeks after hostilities had commenced



and also to know that the German-Hamburg liner Willehad, with a rich cargo on [DOT]board, worth millions of dollars, steamed down the gulf of St. Lawrence, proceeded along the Nova Scotia coast and sought refuge at Portland, while the Niobe was tied up with a chain at her port bow, a chain at her starboard bow, and two chains over her quarter deck so that she could not put to sea. It was also humiliating for Nova Scotians to know that the North-Ger-man-Lloyd steamer Princess Cecelia left Boston a day or two after war commenced with the most valuable cargo ever shipped from that port and with a million dollars of gold in her strong box, and that no effort could be made by the Niobe or by any Canadian cruiser to go out and capture that ship, although fishermen off Cape Sable reported seeing her steam down the Nova Scotia coast and leisurely turn back and make for Portland, Maine.
The Government awoke at last to the fact that something had to be done. They realized that the British Government required all their battleships, cruisers and destroyers to protect their own interests in the North sea and to keep the lanes oi commerce open; consequently they realized that they could not purchase or arrange with Britain for any of her ships. It became necessary for them, therefore, to endeavour to provide ways and means to protect some of the ports on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and they proceeded to waste money in the purchase of a lot of small boats which were utterly useless for defensive purposes. Orders were given to shipbuilding firms all over the country, and boats of the drifter and trawler class were contracted for and feverishly rushed to completion. A number of retired English officers were sent to this country to help organize a Canadian naval service. Naval recruits were asked for, captains and first mates were taken from the merchant marine service and held around Halifax for months drawing pay and doing nothing, for the simple reason that there was nothing for them to do. The story is a disgraceful one and should bring the blush of shame to every Canadian.
In the meantime there were being gathered at Halifax a motley collection oi broken-down tug-boats, gentlemens' yachts, second-hand trawlers and drifters and the new boats which were being launched. A few of these boats were used for gate purposes at Halifax and proved more of a nuisance to the shipping interests of the country than anything else. When it was
fMr. Duff.]
found that Halifax was full of these boats, a base was established at Sydney, and when the war came to a close some seventy-five boats of all kinds were tied up to the wharves in Sydney harbour. I have no hesitation in saying that the large expenditure of money for naval purposes at Sydney harbour was absolutely wasted; that no good resulted from having these boats in that harbour. Owing to their condition they were constantly undergoing repairs, most of them were unseaworthy and were not fit to go outside the headlands. It is true, that in this way they were given something to do.
