Some of these little gasoline patrol boats were sent out to Low Point and held up all Canadian fishing boats or schooners that came to Sydney harbour, instead of allowing them to pass without delay on their way in and out.
One of these boats known as the T. R. 30 was ordered to sea one morning, and on account of the condition of the boat's deck, seven of the seamen refused to proceed to sea unless the deck was caulked. Water had been pouring down the decks into the bunks of these seamen for several days. They reported the matter to their officer, and he reported it to the officer in command at Sydney, who refused to have anything done. These men were court-martialed and sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment, and the mayor of Halifax protested against the sentence. I purpose putting on record the correspondence between the mayor and Mr. Desbarats, Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs. This item first appeared in the Halifax Herald:
Major Hawkins says there were seventy-one prisoners at Rockhead on Sunday.
Rockhead is the Halifax jail or penitentiary, where these boys were incarcerated:
He told this at the Board of Control meeting yesterday, and said further that there were there since August last a number of boys, some of them from good families and environment, who say that they complained at 'Sydney of unseaworthiness of a trawler on which they were serving, were tried there by court martial, brought here in irons and put in the city prison for eighteen months. The mayor said he had written the minister. Hon. Mr. Ballantyne, in reference to the matter. "Shipping laws are severe", said His Worship, "but it strikes me these boys got a raw deal from the Naval Department. They say no naval rules or regulations were read to them." His Worship' was informed that the boys had refused to go. to sea in the trawlers. If they had deserted,, they might have got but ninety days. They were ignorant of what they were doing, he said..
This item must have come to the attention of Mr. Desbarats, Deputy Minister of Naval Affairs, and he wrote Mayor Haw-

kins at Halifax the following letter on January 29, 1919:
Dear Sir:
In the absence of the minister I am answering your letter of the 21st regarding seven seamen from T.R. 30 who were court-martialed and sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment for "wilful disobedience of lawful command."
I do not think there is much justification for the statement that these men were not fairly treated at their trial or were given a raw deal. The men were part of the crew of one of the .trawlers doing convoy work at Sydney in protecting the vessels sailing out of that port. These men refused to take the ship out when she was ordered for duty with the convoy and the mercantile vessels sailed without the protection of this trawler. The offence whs a very serious one and if the convoy had been attacked the absence of this trawler in the line might have allowed of the sinking of one or more of the convoyed ships.
That is the most ridiculous statement 1 ever saw put on paper by a responsible officer, and I say without hesitation there was not in Sydney a patrol boat, not to speak of the T.E. 30, which could convoy any vessel or protect any merchant or other ship. The letter continues:
There was no question as to the seaworthiness of T.R. 30. She is one of a number of similar ships which have proved to be thoroughly seaworthy and staunch. The complaint made by the men was that water leaked from the deck into their quarters and rendered them uncomfortable and insanitary. An inspection was made at the time by the Warrant Shipwright, who reported slight leaks but nothing of a serious kind.
So it is admitted there was some ground for the boys' compla'int. The letter continues:
Even supposing that there had been serious leaks and that a good deal of water leaked into the men's quarters, this would have been no reason for refusing duty and for preventing the ship to take her place in the line and do her share in protecting the convoy.
The men stated that, they were quite aware of the seriousness of refusing duty but notwithstanding this they took the action related above. If men on active service were allowed to refuse duty on acoount of uncomfortable surroundings there would be no need of any defensive or offensive warfare. The offence committed by the men was quite serious, they took the action with full knowledge of its gravity, they pleaded guilty to the charge of disobedience, they were tried in an open court and given every opportunity to present any defence which they might have, and there is no justification for a charge of unfair treatment on the part of the authorities.
These men can hardly be classed as boys, as their ages vary from eighteen to twenty-eight, with an average of twenty-three, and they are therefore quite old enough to realize their [DOT]responsibilities.	.
It is to he regretted that ilt should have been necessary to sentence these men to punish-
139i
ment but it does not seem possible to maintain discipline in a fleet if men are to he allowed to refuse their duty on the grounds of personal disoomfort especially as in this case the discomfort would hardly seem to have been of a serious nature.
I trust these explanations will show that there was good ground for punishing these men and that there was no injustice in the sentence which they received.
Yours truly,
(Signed) G. J. Destoarats,
Deputy Minister.
My understanding of the matter is that these boys were poor boys from the country who knew nothing about military or naval regulations, and if, as Mr. Desbarats says, they pleaded guilty, what
10 p.m. else could they do when they were before the court-martial? I suppose they thought the best thing they could do was to say whatever the court wanted them to say. This, letter of Mr. Desbarats did not satisfy Mayor Hawkins, and on February 1, 1919, he replied as follows to Mr. Desbarats:
Dear Sir,-In answer to your letter of the 29th ultimo, it is my desire that my letter of the 21st ultimo regarding the seven seamen from the T.R. 30, who were court-martialed and sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment for "willful disobedience of lawful command," he placed before a responsible minister in the absence of the minister of your department.
_ There has been a good deal of feeling aroused in this community on account of the way ip which these seamen were treated ; the sentence imposed is looked upon as very much out of proportion, compared with other sentences of officers who have been court martialed.
The story of a certain Lieutenant Legatt, late commanding Officer of the II.M.C.S. Hoche-laga, who was court martialed and honourably discharged from service for cowardice, has been mentioned in the public press. It -would he interesting to know, as the court martial was held on these boys on the Hochelaga, if this officer had anything to do in passing sentence upon the offenders from the T.R. 30.
There are other instances where it would seem to show that there is a law for officers and another for seamen.
Yours trply,
(Signed) A. C. Hawkins,
Mayor.
In view of these facts, if these boys have not already been released, the acting Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. A. K. Maclean) should draw the matter to the attention of the minister and have these boys released from jail immediately, and make proper restitution. An hon. member asked the Department of Naval Affairs for some information in regard to this trawler upon which these boys served, and it was necessary for him to ask the question several times before he could get very much in-

formation. Some of the questions asked by this member were as follows:
Was trawler No. 30 in the service of the Canadian Navy Department during the summer of 1918?
The answer was "yes."
If so, were any refits necessary to this boat during the summer of 1918?
The answer was "no." This is the summer the boys were sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment.
On what date was this boat laid up for refits?
The answer was:
Answered by No. 2.
There were no refits, said the department.
Where was trawler No. 30 on August 9, 1918?
The answer was:
At Sydney, under routine lay-up.
If there was nothing wrong with this boat, why was it lying at Sydney under routine lay-up unless that was the excuse for having all the boats tied up at the wharves at Sydney? But I have absolute information that these answers are not correct, and I say that on August 14, 1918, the Sydney Foundry Company completed the work of caulking and pitching the deck of this trawler, the amount of the account being $284. This was the boat from which these seven poor seamen were court mar-tialed and sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment, and yet within a fortnight after they were sentenced, this boat was laid up for refits and the deck caulked and pitched by the Sydney Foundry Company at a cost to this country of $284. Let us go a little further in this matter. Who were the gentlemen who court martialed these seven poor seamen from a fishing hamlet on the Atlantic coast? There was a steamer on naval duty called the Hochelaga, which was commanded by a certain gentleman and which was sent to sea on patrol duty. The look-out on this naval patrol boat one morning sighted a submarine; he reported the matter to the captain, and the captain, who was in charge of eight or ten small boats in addition to his own, at once put up signals to return to port, and instead of stopping and endeavouring to get that submarine or be sunk in the attempt, the captain of the Hochelaga deliberately turned tail and proceeded back to port. This captain is one of the three men who sentenced those seven poor Nova Scotia fishermen to eighteen months in the penitentiary. It is true that after the Hochelagf
fMr. Duff.]
returned to port and the naval authorities came into possession of the fact that the captain had acted in a cowardly manner they discharged him. But why in the name of common sense was he allowed to go with an honourable discharge, while these seven poor Nova Scotian fishermen were sen tenced to eighteen months at Eockhead? Is that fair play? Is that in keeping with the traditions of the British navy? No; and I say action should be taken to release these boys from Eockhead and make whatever restitution is possible.
We have endeavoured to get information from the Department of Naval Service this session with regard to some of the steamers it employs, but in nearly every case the answer has been unsatisfactory or contradictory. I think the truth of the matter is-that the Government are ashamed of the whole sorry mess of bungling extravagance and mismanagement of the naval affairs of this country since the war started.
To show the uselessness of the steamers composing this so-called navy, let me give one or two illustrations. On a fine summer day in 1918 the oil-tanker Lux Blanca, having discharged her cargo at the Imperial Oil works at Dartmouth, got up steam for sea. She was an American boat manned by American sailors and captained by an American ship-master. She proceeded out of the harbour and headed westward. When thirty-five miles west of Sambro island, the lookout sighted the periscope of a submarine. Let me say at this point that previous to this date the naval authorities at Halifax and Ottawa knew there was a submarine on the Nova Scotia coast, yet nothing was done. There were no patrol boats outside the headlands of Halifax harbour. When the lookout sighted the periscope of the submarine what did the captain of this oil-tanker do? Did he turn tail as the captain of the Hochelaga did? No. He had a gun forward and another gun aft, and he had these guns manned and trained on the periscope of the submarine. He gave instructions to the wireless operator to send a message to the Halifax station that he was attacked by a submarine and to send help. He turned his ship towards Halifax harbour and fought that submarine for three hours. The message was sent to Halifax about two in the afternoon, but, Mr. Chairman, not a boat left Halifax to go to that ship's assistance, and the result was that some of the crew of that oil tanker were killed, some were wounded, the ship was sunk, and the rest of the crew had to

[DOT]take to the boats. I admit that there were no ships in our naval fleet that could have sunk the submarine, but they could have done this: When that S.O.S. call came the naval authorities should have sent those boats to sea. I do not blame the captains or crews of those boats or drifters; I lay the blame on the men in charge of the naval base at Halifax, most of whom do not belong to this country, but were sent over from England after their period of usefulness there had,finished. Every man who knows anything about the business says that when that S.O.S. call came the naval authorities should have sent those boats out to sea because, whilst they may not have been able to sink the submarine, the minute the submarine sighted their smoke on the horizon, the good black smoke from Sydney coal, she would have disappeared and the oil tanker would have been saved. While this vessel was being sunk the naval officials at Halifax were trifling at pink teas and playing bridge whist. That is the way we were protected on the Nova Scotia coast.
Let me give another instance-I have five hundred pages here, and it will be impossible for me to give it all. The Lady Evelyn was one of the best boats in the patrol service. She had first class equipment; in fact, naval officers tell me that she was the only vessel in the fleet that could have engaged a submarine. While this submarine was off the Nova Scotia coast, the Lady Evelyn, the best equipped vessel in the fleet, was sent to the Magdalen islands to deliver six lead pencils to the wireless operator there. There were at this time some American destroyers also on our coast, and about the same day the Lady Evelyn went to the Magdalen islands to deliver the lead pencils, an American destroyer was off Cape Canso. This was twenty-four hours before the fishing vessels were sunk in those waters. This American destroyer received a call to return to Halifax. When the commander of the destroyer received the call he wired back that he had information a submarine was in his zone. Nevertheless, he was ordered back to Halifax on some paltry excuse, and when he got there he was sent out on convoy with the ship that was to take Prince Arthur of Cbn-naught to England. Whilst the fishermen were left to row a hundred and forty miles, this American destroyer was sailing out with Prince Arthur. Is that the way to treat the people of this country? That is what actually happened.
Let me'go a little further. Two German submarines came across the water last May. They operated first on the American coast. The Naval Department here knew all about them, and I might say that I sent several telegrams about the matter myself to Mr, Desbarats. These submarined sunk a number of American ships off the American coast, and gradually worked down the Bay of Fundy sinking vessels belonging to merchants of St, John, New Brunswick, some of them new vessels with valuable cargoes, The submarines next appeared off Cape Sable, then off Shelburne and proceeded down the Nova Scotia coast. In the town of Liverpool, at the time, three large vessels were preparing for sea. There were four or five in my home town, and several in the Lahave river preparing for sea, and to proceed to foreign ports These captains, notwithstanding the fact that they knew that the submarine was coming down the Nova iScotia coast, proceeded to sea on their voyage. They did not fear the submarine; they did not fear the Germans. No; it was the patrol boats and those others who were the ones that were making all the trouble. This submarine after destroying the Lux Blanca, proceeded down the co'ast off Canso. You will probably remember, Mr. Chairman, that the first ship she sank was a trawler belonging to parties in the constituency of the hon. Acting Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. A. K. Maclean). While the American destroyer that was sent down by the United States to protect our coast was sent to Halifax to convoy a ship on which was Prince Arthur of Connaught, the submarine sank five or six Nova Scotia vessels and one American vessel, and the fishermen were ordered into their dories. Hon. members may not all know what a dory is. It is a small boat about fifteen feet long capable of containing only two men. These fishermen were given five minutes to leave the ship and take to their dories and then had to row for two days and two nights before reaching Canso. And this was the kind of protection we were receiving from the naval service of this country. The submarine proceeded down the St. Pierre banks and this is the time the Hochelaga turned tail, when the submarine was about 50 miles off Sydney harbour. As I say, she proceeded down the St. Pierre banks and several more fishing vessels anchored there were sunk. The crews had to row about 45 miles to St. Pierre and arriving there-I think there were about 110 men altogether-the Governor of St. Pierre realized that provisions were short and that it was advis-

able to despatch these men as quickly as possible, and cabled, I presume, to the Ottawa authorities, because shortly afterwards instructions were forwarded to Sydney to despatch one of the patrol boats to St. Pierre to bring the Lunenburg county fishermen to that port. My information is, and 1 believe it is correct, that on that occasion, because the boat was unseaworthy, the whole crew refused to go to sea and the captain had to get an entire new crew, except himself and the wireless operator. I do not know where he got them from, but I am informed that on the way back from St. Pierre to North Sydney, although it was not very rough, every man jack aboard the trawler was sick, except the captain and the wireless operator, and the fishing crew had to do the crew's work and help bring the patrol from St. Pierre to North Sydney. That is the kind of naval service we get in Canada.
Then they tell a story, and it is a true one, that when one of the fishing vessels was coming up in the fog off Halifax harbour the man on the lookout did not see the patrol boats, but he said he smelled ham and eggs, and shortly after the fog lifted there were about ten of these patrol boats in the shelter of Sambro Light. They did not come alongside the ship and tell them that there was a submarine in the vicinity, but allowed that vessel with twenty valuable lives to proceed on her way without notifying the captain of the danger. It seems to me that the least they might have done was to apprise him of the presence of the submarine so that the captain could put into Halifax harbour. Another method that was practiced was to get men for these ships by robbing the merchant marine. Every vessel that came to Halifax from a foreign voyage with crews that had been facing the submarine in the submarine zone in Spanish waters, in the Mediterranean and nearly every place else where the submarine was most in evidence, these men having faced these grave dangers for six, nine and twelve months, on arriving at Halifax they were arrested by the military police and put in jail. I know of one case-and I can . mention more-in which the mate of ,a ship called the Win the War was arrested and put in jail by the military police. The mate of a vessel that arrived in Halifax one Saturday morning was arrested and put in the lockup over Sunday, taken to Aldershot and kept in custody for a week until the owners of his vessel got him out. We are supposed to emulate the example of Great Britain, and yet this condition of affairs existed in spite of the fact that Great Bri-
LMr. Duff,]
tain, gave every encouragement to the members of the British marine. I have in my hand what is known as a notice to mariners for 1918 in which appears the following:
Maintenance of British Shipping.
Officers and Seamen of the Mercantile Marine (except Stewards on Passenger Vessels) are included in the list of certified occupations issued under the Military Service Act, 1916, as persons who are engaged in work of national importance and are entitled to exemption from Military Service. If Officers or Seamen receive notices to present theipselves for military service they should return the notices to the military authorities claiming exemption.
The efficient maintenance of the Mercantile Marine is of vital national importance, and Masters, Officers and Seamen should remain with their ships, and should not leave the merchant service to join the Army.
Why was that not done in this country? Was it not necessary that we should have our merchant marine available to carry our products? I think the Government would have been well advised had they followed this clause in the British Merchant Marine Act, and not arrested our boys who were returning to see their parents for a week or two after long sea voyages. I have in mind a case in my county of a young fisherman who came hoihe last September and who was arrested by the military police, although he says that at a public meeting held in 1917, at which an official of the Militia Department spoke and made the announcement that the fishermen and farmers would no{ be taken, as conscription was intended only for the province of Quebec. This man was arrested, and the reason he gave for not having obeyed the regulations of the Military Service Act was the statement that this official of the department had made that he would not be conscripted. The boy, of course, was guilty under the Military Service Aot; there is no question about that. He was taken to Halifax and before a court-martial of military officers, this pooT fisherman, who did not iknow the law and for whom there was some excuse, was sentenced to two years' hard labour in the penitentiary,-a splendid' man who had supported his mother from the time he was twelve years of age. He had engaged in fishing on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, and off the coast of Nova Scotia from the age of twelve, and had kept a widowed mother and two sisters. He certainly did not know anything about the law, and yet a court-martial consisting of three supposedly intelligent officers, deliberately sentenced him to two years' imprisonment. However, the boy had a few frieds and they certioraried

his case to Judge Drysdale. I have not Judge Drysdaile's decision before me at this moment, but I may say that the judge decided that the boy 'Should be released. After his release he went to the barracks and told the officers that he wanted his clothes, which consisted of a pair of long rubber boots, stable overalls and an old cap, in which he had been arrested, handcuffed and taken to Halifax. But he demanded -his clothes from the militia authorities, and putting them on he walked the streets of Halifax for three days, and to every man he met he said he would not go home until the Militia Department sent him home. He went every morning to the barracks and insisted on being sent home, and at last they were so ashamed that the officers paid his fare home.
Speaking of the purchases of ships foT the so-called Canadian navy, I would like to know why the officers of the Naval Department did not adopt the suggestion of Mr. J. K. L. Ross. When the war broke out. Mr. Ross, in conversation with a certain naval officer, thought that something should be done for the defence of Canada. He went to one of the shipyards in the province of Quebec-I think it was Vickers, but I am not quite sure-and said to the manager, " How long will it take you to build five cruisers of the Bristol type?'' The manager gave Mr. Ross the information, and at his own expense, he hired a 'special train, journeyed to Ottawa, and laid the matter before the naval authorities. He offered to pay for one of these cruisers if the Government would build the other four, but his offer was turned down and he went home in disgust. When matters were in a serious condition on the Nova Scotia coast, and we could not get any protection for our shipping from the Canadian Government, I am very pleased, indeed, to say that after an earnest telegram was sent to the Department of Naval Affairs-and I want to eonvey to the member for Halifax the credit for what was done after strong representations were made to him by two business men at Halifax-the Naval Department realized that they would again have to go with their hat in hand to the American naval authorities for protection, and very shortly afterwards one or more American naval destroyers were sent to the Nova Scotia coast to protect Canadian shipping. Now, whilst I am very pleased, indeed, that we had the protection of American naval vessels-we owe a debt of gratitude to the American people and the American Government for what they did for us; there is no
question about it, their destroyers saved a lot of our ships because one of them went as far as the Grand Banks of Newfoundland and notified the fishing vessels to get into port-I say it is a shame that we should have had to depend upon the American navy to protect our coasts, our fishermen, and our shipping. Let me tell the Committee something else.- This is a personal matter, but my reason for telling it now is that I have never been able to discover the name of the captain of the destroyer who did the good work. One Saturday night I received a telephone message from Liverpool, and the gentleman on the wire informed me that he was the captain of an American destroyer. He said that a Lunenburg vessel, a foreign-going ship, was drifting five miles off Gull Rock with a disabled rudder. He said, " I left my sister ship out there to protect her, while I came in to give you the news. The captain asked me to request you to send out a tugboat to tow him either to Liverpool or Halifax." I told him to wait for an hour until I ascertained if I could get a tugboat at Yarmouth or Halifax. I kept the telephone busy but failed to secure a tugboat. I' then telephoned the captain of the American destroyer that I could not get any assistance, whereupon he said: "I will return to my ship and both of our destroyers will stand by the disabled vessel until you can send out assistance." I managed to get a towboat from Halifax the next afternoon, but by the time she arrived the American commander had commandeered an American fishing vessel, attached it to the stern of the Lunenburg ship, and fastening hawsers to their destroyers had towed the disabled vessel into Liverpool. I have never been able to find out who the captain of this destroyer was. The American Government so far have rendered no bill for the services rendered"; doubtless if they intended to do so they would have done it long ago. Now I want to express my gratification to the American commanders of these destroyers for 'the splendid assistance which they rendered. Undoubtedly these destroyers rendered splendid aid in keeping submarines away and protecting Canadian shipping, a duty which properly devolved upon the Government of this country, which should have had proper ships in Nova Scotia waters for that purpose.
Did the Americans perform any other service for us? They certainly did. They established airplane, or seaplane, bases at Halifax and North Sydney, and were about

to establish another at Shelburne when hostilities ceased. But a base was established at Halifax and on the first flight of one of the squadrons, in order to show what the seaplanes could do, the route followed was via the towns from Halifax to Yarmouth; and I had 'the honour, Mr. Chairman, as mayor of the town of Lunenburg, to receive the first letter, written Dy the Premier of Nova 'Scotia to me, which was ever delivered at that town by seaplane. These seaplanes went from Lunenburg to Liverpool, Lockeport, Shelburne and Yarmouth, and the people of the different towns along the coast turned out in full force to do honour to the brave American airmen who were protecting our coast and stopping the depredations of German submarines, which duty we should have performed ourselves. What a humiliating position for Canada 'to be placed in, to be dependent for protection on the sea and in the air to American destroyers and American airplanes.
In addition to the expenditure of $31,000,000 for naval war purposes, the Auditor General's Report sets forth that in 1918 the sum of $209,296 was spent on the dockyard and naval college at Halifax, principally for frills, furbelows, and pink teas-At Esquimalt, $244,554 was paid for gold braid and brass buttons. When I read the Auditor General's Report and saw - what this amount was for I was shocked and disgusted. For clerks, stenographers, telephones and telephone operators the sum of $168,000 was spent last year at the Halifax dockyard and naval establishment. Nine thousand, seven hundred and twelve pairs of boots were purchased from Ames Holden and the Amherst Boot and Shoe Company; 5,097 silk handkerchiefs were purchased at about one dollar each. There were purchased 57,605 pounds of ordinary soap, and 3,403 pounds of Castile soap, presumably for the lime-juicers. These are some of the items appearing in the Report. It is impossible for me to give the full details of the expenditure for these purposes, but the Auditor General's Report is worth the serious perusal of every member of the Committee. Another item which appears in the Report is $665 allowance for clergy. Mr. Chairman, I regret to say that this amount was paid to Presbyterian clergymen as well as clergymen of every other denomination, and I am ashamed that Presbyterian clergymen should have taken this money. These very Presbyterian clergymen in 1917, when I was a candidate for Parliament, said that I, and others like me, were pro-German, were disloyal and traitors fair. Duff.l
to the country. These were the clergymen who were going to save the country. I understand there are about forty clergymen in the city of Halifax and they are not overworked. These men who were so extremely loyal in the 1917 election should have gone out on board the Niobe and given their services free-that is the least they might have done. It seems a shame and a disgrace to me that ministers who endeavour to teach us to be patriotic should take the country's money for going on the Niobe and giving religious services to the sailors.
Then to show some of the acts of gross carelessness on the part of the Naval Department at Halifax I want to refer for a minute to the Halifax explosion. On December 6, 1917, the whole country from Halifax to Vancouver was shocked when it heard that Halifax had been blown up by an explosion and that some two thousand people had lost their lives and between twenty and thirty thousand injured. It is almost impossible to believe that so many people were injured, but it is a fact that between twenty and thirty thousand of the population of that city were -more or less injured by the explosion. What happened?
The steamer Mont Blanc arrived at Halifax one fine December morning. A steamer named the Imo had received instructions the night before to proceed to sea. Orders were given to the Mont Blanc to proceed up the harbour and as the Imo was coming through the narrow channel between Dartmouth and Halifax, a collision occurred, and the high explosives on the Mont Blanc created the tremendous devastation with which we are all familiaT. An investigation followed, but nothing came of it-at any rate, whatever information the' Government secured it never published it. There were plenty of rumours current, one being to the effect that the collision was due to neglect on the part of one of the naval officers in charge-and it is a fact that a naval officer was discharged from the service, he having given conflicting orders. I contend that there was absolutely no necessity for the Mont Blanc to come up to the harbour, and the naval authorities had no right to allow her to come up, -there being plenty of space in -the eastern passage to lay, whilst awaiting orders to proceed. Not only that ship but other ships containing high explosives were allowed to come up to the middle of the city both before and after this disaster and if there had been a German spy on board he could have blown up the whole city.
What do we find about this matter? I will not give my own version, but I will

quote from what a good Unionist newspaper says. This is something that happened after the explosion and after the naval authorities should have been on their job, if they were not when that disastrous collision occurred. The Halifax Herald of March 12, 1917, contained the following:
Further investigation by The Halifax Herald [DOT]in shipping and1 pilotage circles yesterday has brought additional and conclusive evidence that there must be a shake-up of no meagre dimensions at Ottawa. The pilots' story that a steamer laden with high explosives was allowed to lay in the fairway of the harbour one day last week for seven hours, was fully confirmed, and in getting the confirmation other details of a most startling nature were disclosed.
The Halifax Herald' is scrupulously careful to abide by the rules of the censorship and anything calculated to furnish information to the enemy is gladly withheld from publication. There is not a man familiar with marine affairs at this port, not a Nova Scotia captain who has gladly given his services to the work of naval patrol, not a master mariner who regularly brings in and takes out his steamer, but what has a story to tell of stupidity, of pigheaded-mess, of bungling in connection With the affairs of the port, and, following up these stories, the trail leads directly to Ottawa and reveals a heterogeneous bunch of incompetents who may know the ways of society, who may be able to judge aright the merits of various blends of wine, but who certainlly do not know the ways of ships and are not able to judge the competence of those whom they place in charge.
In times of peace we should not have such men at the head of affairs of a maritime nature. To have them in such position in these awful days of war is evidence of a laxity on the part of our people, a laxity which has already led to fatal consequences and which should, perchance, a break be made through the British fleet, lead to awful disaster. God forbid that a change at Ottawa be withheld until such a time comes.
It took one of the greatest disasters the world has ever known, to partially arouse those in authority, but those who were in supreme authority then are still in authority.
I repeat, that is from the Halifax Herald, a paper edited by no other than one William Dennis, a member of the honourable Senate of Canada.
As far as I am personally concerned, I have watched this matter for the last four or five years, and I want to say that I do not hold the present 'Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Ballantyne) responsible in any great degree. I believe he took charge of this thing when it was in such a mess that he realized that nothing could be done by him. I do not wish to imply that all the naval officers were incompetent. There were a number of bright, young Canadian officers scattered through the fleet, and a large number of marines and bluejackets, who, if they had been given a chai>ce, would have distinguished themselves and brought
honour to Canada, but these men were not given an opportunity so to do.
The naval conditions on the Atlantic coast were of such a disgraceful nature that it was in the mouths of everybody, and I have gathered a large amount of information which it would take up too much time to place before this Committee. The matter is of such a serious nature that I consider an investigation should be held, and I here and now ask for a parliamentary committee to be appointed, and I have the proof to place before any investigating body that [DOT]may be appointed. I had an opportunity, (Mr. Chairman, of discussing this matter with a naval officer and a number of sailors, and I got the former to give me his opinion why the naval affairs of this country were in such a disgraceful condition. He gave me ,a statement, which I will now read:-
I, the undersigned Charles Otis Julian, of the city of Vancouver, in the province of British Columbia, Lieutenant Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve, hereby solemnly declare:
That the Borden Government knowing the imminent possibilities of the outbreak of war showed culpable neglect in not having the Canadian naval dockyards in Halifax and Esquimalt in a proper state of efficiency.
That the dockyards were in a deplorable state of decay and neglect, the wharves and jetties being in need of repair, the buildings and store houses being old and unsuitable, the stores depleted and the general equipment inadequate and an no way suited to carry on effective war-time operations.
That the Borden Government showed further culpable neglect before the outbreak of war in allowing the Niobe and Rainbow to remain out of commission without proper equipment in vifew of the threatening situation in Europe. The Niobe at the outbreak of war was moored at Halifax and would have remained an ineffectual fighting ship had she not obtained crews from the Imperial ships, Algerine and Shearwater; the Rainbow would have been in the same predicament had she not obtained sufficient ratings to man her from the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserves then in process of formation and a nucleus crew from the Atlantic station.	,
That the Fishery Protection Service vessels of Canada as equipped and manned were totally inadequate to offer any effective protection to our cities on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
That the Borden Government showed culpable neglect in not encouraging and ordering the formation of an effective Royal Navy Canadian Volunteer Reserve and that as far back as three years prior to the outbreeak of war many representations had been made to the Government without result for the recognition and proper equipment of the force (then struggling in process of formation; and that after this force had come into being with scarce government aid, the Director of Naval Service, acting on instructions from his Government proceeded to disband the Naval Volunteers of Canada, and that a majority of men who had joined this force with a pure volunteer spirit were encouraged to leave the force and join the

C.E.F. That in the city of Quebec, directly after the outbreak of hostilities, on instructions from the department more than one hundred naval ratings were recruited carried on drill and such duties as were allotted to them by the S.N.O. at that port. These men were without equipment of any kind. Thirty-three days after its formation this force was disbanded and discharged. That no provision was made anywhere in Canada towards naval recruiting. In Toronto private efforts succeeded in recruliting a considerable number of naval ratings who were despatched to Imperial and R.C.N. establishments. Although in the British Isles directly after the outbreak of hostilities recruiting for ratings for naval brigades was carried on, no provision was made in Canada for recruiting for the navy although repeated appeals were made to the Government to do so.
That the Borden Government showed culpable neglect at the very outbreak of hostilities when unarmed enemy merchantmen were in close proximity to our coast in not endeavouring to capture or destroy these ships. The Government were repeatedly advised of the presence of these ships but made no effort to capture them although they had suitable ships available for this purpose.
That the Borden Government showed unfair discrimination from the outbreak of hostilities to the signing of the armistice against native born Canadians in all senior appointments both ashore and afloat in the Canadian Naval Service. That in the larger ships of the Canadian Patrol Fleet only one native born Canadian has been in command. In almost every instance these ships carried in the position of Navigator or First Lieutenant eprfectly capable Canadian officers. That the records of the shore establishment show that these bases were elaborately overmanned by retired, and in many cases incapable R.N. or R.N.R. English officers. The same condition prevailed at the naval headquarters at Ottawa. That the graduates of the Royal Naval College of Canada of sufficient seniority and entirely capable of taking command of Canadian patrol ships who were on loan to the R.N. were not recalled and given the opportunity to serve in the defence of their own country.
That the Borden Government's actions have occasioned a general spirit of discontent and resentment among *the officers and men in the Canadian Naval Service. That promotions have been unfairly allotted and positions of trust have been given to men of unknown and questionable ability. That seniority and previous experience have been most shamefully overlooked in numerous instances and throughout the rank and file of the service a feeling of discontent, contempt and distrust has always been entertained against the authorities at Ottawa. That the department has repeatedly broken faith most shamefully with officers and men, the notable instances being in the case of the treatment of mates. In the beginning these officers were promised toy the department that they would rank with, tout after a sublieutenant R.N.C.V.R. in accordance with clause 13 relative to rank as found in the K. R. & O. After they had served some considerable period, however, and without any cause they were reduced by Order in Council two grades lower and ranked with bandmasters, masters-at-arms, boatswains, etc. That in the case of chief skippers R.C.N., these men all holding coastwise and foreign seagoing tickets were

induced to join the service with the promise of a rate of pay of $3.50 per day. After serving some considerable time an order was issued reducing their pay to $3.00 per day. That in the case of W.T. operators, these officers were, without any apparent reason, unjustly denied any separation allowance. A considerable number were in the service before the Order in Council to this effect was passed, and these men were discriminated against in a most shameful manner. The pay for this branch of the service was ridiculously small considering that these officers had to bear a great part of their own expenses in the matter of messing and clothing. On the larger ships it was necessary for operators to live with wardroom officers and pay their mess bills out of their small pay. Until 1918 no proper school was established for their training, consequently many were unable to qualify as fourth class operators and were forced to remain "Learners" for an unreasonable length of time. The pay of a "Learner" was $22.50 per month.
(1)	In the beginning the rate of pay in the R.N.C.V.R. was fixed much lower than that given to men in the C.E.F., and no separation allowance was granted, enlistments to the Navy were therefore reduced to a minimum and great dissatisfaction prevailed among the men in the service.
(2)	That the Naval Service repeatedly made promises to mem on enlistment in connection with rank, promotions, rate of pay and conditions of service which they later failed to fulfil.
(3)	For more than a year and a half after the outbreak of the war men wearing the Canadian Naval uniform were not allowed reduced fares or any special privileges by the transportation companies in Canada, while at the same time such were enjoyed by the men in the C.E.F.
(4)	That it would appear that the Borden Government in the manner of the treatment of the men in the Canadian Navy were pursuing a policy of deliberately creating a feeling of dissatisfaction in order to justify their prewar contention that Canada could not man and maintain a navy of her own. The result of this policy is very apparent as such a feeling still exists.
That the Borden Government showed culpable lack of foresight since the beginning of the war in the method it pursued in chartering vessels, exorbitant rentals being paid for .inferior craft, so much so that in many instances the charter money as time went on amounted to much more than the actual value of some of the crafts in question. That those crafts were supplied with coal and water, besides being kept in ship-shape condition at the expense of the Government, gun-crews and signal ratings being placed on board and utilized by the owners of the craft. And with exception of a few large harbour tugs the boats proved inadequate for the duties assigned to them.
As regards small craft, the iBorden Government expended large sums of money' in a ridiculous and wasteful manner in chartering or purchasing at exorbitant rates, numerous motor boats and other small craft which were to be found at the bases at Halifax and Sydney and Esquimalt. These boats were continuously out of repair, their up-keep amounting annually to large sums. These boats being used principally for the convenience of senior officers ashore and their wives and families.

Over seventy per cent of these boats could have been dispensed with had this branch of the service been conducted in an efficient manner.
The Borden Government did not pursue the policy of other Overseas Dominions in despatching naval ratings for duty overseas-until obliged to do so by pressure in the House -and then only in a half-hearted, manner. Then the Deputy Minister, the Director of Naval Service and the Admiral Superintendent at Esquimau expressed personally their displeasure and disapproval of the policy of sending amy such naval ratings overseas.
That throughout the entire war no policy appears to have existed in regard to the vitally important work of patrolling and convoying off the coasts of Canada. As a result of their lack of policy and unpreparedness when the coasts of Canada were seriously menaced by submarines an appeal had to be made to the United States for the despatch of craft capable of protecting our coasts. That our large patrol vessels with one exception proved to be old, out of date vessels deficient in speed and gun power and were all out of order. In convoy work the Canadian fleet could not venture far from their bases and it is on record that not one flotilla ever despatched successfully carried out the orders assigned them.
That the Borden Government showed culpable neglect in regard to the gunnery of the patrol fleet, many of the boats being fitted for a considerable period with obsolete guns and no provision being made for the proper training of gun crews under experienced officers and it was not until the fall of 1917 that this most important branch of the service was taken in hand and a gunnery commander appointed. This officer experienced great difficulty in carrying out his work owing to reluctance of the Department to supply them with proper ordinance and gear.
That although the traffic regulations of the Port of Halifax were under the sole supervision of the Naval authorities proper orders were never promulgated and such regulations as were in effect were carried out with laxity.
That although the calamity that overtook the Port of Halifax on December 6th, 19117, was accidental nevertheless there can be no doubt that the actual cause can be traced to the inefficient and careless officers in charge of the Canadian Naval base at Halifax.
That many acts of heroism performed by Canadian Naval ratings received no recognition although officers and men from vessels of the Royal Navy then lying in the harbour performing similar acts received prompt recognition and declaration from their Government.

Lieut. R.N.C.V.R.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think that under the circumstances, and having regard to what I have said, there should be a full and complete investigation into naval affairs in Canada during the last four years. Furthermore, I have no hesitation in saying that owing to the black eye which has been administered to the navy, it is too late now to endeavour to do anything to put naval affairs in Canada on a satisfactory basis. At the time of the Soudanese war, when the question of sending help
to Britain was discussed in this Parliament, Sir John A. Macdonald used the expression: " Not a dollar, not a man." I repeat that statement [DOT] now without any hesitation. I say in all seriousness that Canada should not spend one dollar on naval matters for the next few years at least. One reason is that our financial condition will not warrant it, and even if we wished to do so we could not vote sufficient money to build or to purchase naval boats which would be Of any service in time of trouble.
Because of its inefficiency, the Naval Department at Ottawa should be closed up, the officers in charge of it should be paid off and the offices closed. Canada has nothing to lose by doing this, and a large amount of money would be saved the taxpayers.
In my opinion Parliament can do only one of two things: Appropriate $100,000,000 at least, to build and equip an efficient navy, or else not spend one dollar. I do not think that in our present financial condition we can afford to spend the large amount which I have mentioned; consequently I say that not one dollar should be spent and not one man engaged at the present time under the excuse and pretence that we are doing something for naval affairs in this country. Sell off the useless trawlers, drifters and patrol boats, clear up the mes£ and make the * best of a bad job.
It might be said, of course, that we have the naval bases at Halifax and Esquimalt, and that they should be kept up. My answer to that is this: If the British Government require Halifax and Esquimalt for naval bases and for coaling purposes, they should take them over and operate them at their own expense. We certainly cannot do it, and I have no hesitation in asking that the whole idea be abandoned.

The statements made by the hon. member (Mr. Duff) with regard to expenditures in connection with naval affairs in Canada are of such a serious character that we should at least have some explanation from the minister before this clause is adopted.	[DOT]
, We have the statement made here by . the hon. member, not as his own, but as a declared statement by an officer who was one of the men in charge at Esquimalt at the time, I believe, and who professes to make a declaration, equal to a statement on oath, as to what has been taking place in connection with the handling of the navy, not only on the coast of British Columbia, but at Halifax, ISydney and other

places. We have not, so far, had a word of explanation from the Government. There may be some minister or other hon. member who* can give us some explanation about this matter, but we have not had a word of explanation, and we are asked to vote $350,000,000, a large part of which is going to be paid out in connection with work of this class. While we are all anxious to get along as fast as we can with the business of this session, including the voting of money, this (Committee and the House and the country are entitled to some explanation as to the charges put forward in respect to the management of this very important department of Government. 'It is well known, in the part of the country from which I come, which is in the same province as the constituency represented by the hon. member (Mr. Duff), that moneys were simply squandered right and left; that every sort of a boat that would float at all was either purchased or hired, and that it was the sheerest mockery the piles of ships that were in each others' way in the harbour of Sydney during the last year or two doing nothing in the world except paying out money to men who were friendly to the Government and who had craft of this kind -to sell or hire. Without some departmental head here able to answer these questions, it would be useless to make-any further charges than those already put before the Committee by the hon. member for Lunenburg, and I do not wish to take up time of re-stating what has been so well said by him. But it is the duty of the Government, and particularly of the minister in charge of this Bill, if he cannot give this explanation himself, to let this matter "stand until the minister who is capable of giving the explanation is here and can tell us how many vessels were purchased or hired; from whom vessels were purchased or hired; what was the necessity of hiring vessels; how many vessels we still own; and what are they worth; and what the Government intends doing with them? I suggested to the Minister of Naval Affairs that such of the 11 p.m. vessels as are equal to the kind of work, should, if possible, be converted into fishing craft. The Canadian people would get more value and better results from those vessels in that way than in any other. I do not know that this is the occasion to discuss that, but I am mentioning it in the presence of so many ministers, that they may have at least one constructive idea in connection with the handling of those boats. I am told that [Mr. McKenzie. 1
many of the boats can be sold to advantage to fishermen who, perhaps, may not be able to pay the whole of the money at once, but a scheme could be arranged by which the Government would be sure of obtaining its money and a fishing fleet of fine proportions, well equipped, would be established on both the Atlantic and the Pacific. If this matter is inquired into at all, we shall be able to get some information from the minister on that score.
At an early stage in the evening, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) made some statements in connection with the furnishing of money for trade purposes. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) thought that he was making a very clever answer when he told us that we were perfectly justified in voting J25,-000,000 of the people's money to Rumania, because Rumania was in debt to Great Britain and that we were in debt to _ Great Britain and the United States, and in order to square our bills with Great Britain and the United States, we should allow Rumania to become indebted to us. If that is a business proposition by which there shall be accorded any satisfaction in the payment of debts between Rumania and Great Britain, Great Britain and ourselves and ourselves and the United States, it is a system that I never heard of before and that I do not understand. The hon. member sat down absolutely satisfied with himself as having solved the whole problem and having justified the borrowing by Canada of $25,000,000 somewhere and passing that over to Rumania in order that Rumania might become indebted to us. If that is business, I shall be glad to have it more fully explained by the minister if he shall deem it proper to make any further observations in connection with this Bill.
There are different ways of promoting trade. When we were in pow'er in this country we promoted trade in the usual way. We wanted to have trade with people who. were willing to pay either in kind or in cash for our goods. In 1911, the situation in this country was excellent, but we wanted to make it better and we launched upon a comprehensive trade arrangement with the people of the United States and other countries where we could get proper trade and where we would have exchange of our goods for theirs or get their money for our goods. That was not good enough for the statesmen who are to-day in charge of affairs, and they turned it down. What have they given to us instead of it? They have given us an

absolutely new idea in trade, namely, that we are to furnish our own money and that we are to buy our own goods, and after we have bought our goods from ourselves, we are to pass them over without any security whatever to a foreign country. Will the minister explain how it is that we are going to get wealthy in that way? Supposing a man furnishes a customer with $5 to buy a pair of boots, the man comes in to his store and buys the boots and he passes over to the [DOT] merchant his own $5. The merchant has his 35 back in his till, but the boots are gone and he has nothing for them. I see many hardheaded business men sitting in front of me, and I should like them to explain how we are going to grow wealthy and expand and develop the country by such a system of trade.
The idea of a man lifting himself by his boot straps has always seemed the most ridiculous thing we could imagine, but I think such a feat is just as easily possible as the making of this country wealthy and prosperous upon the system of trade, and business generally, that is followed by this Government, and which is applauded by its Supporters as a new device which will overcome all the trade ills that the state is heir to. As a matter of fact, we have not got the money to give, but we are undertaking to find it in some way, and pass it off in the manner I have mentioned. 'I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that whether or not this will be a bribe to the manufacturers of this country, to the big combines, the big friends who own the Government according to the Government's own friends, it is capable ol being a bribe. What is happening? The Manufacturers' Association and the men engaged in big business come to the Government and say: " We want more trade. We want more money put in circulation. What are you going to do about it?" The Government says: " If you can get anybody to buy your goods we will pay for them." That is a magnificent proposition. The manufacturer is not asked what his price is, where he will deliver the goods, or anything of that kind; he is simply told by the Government: "We care not what you produce, so long as it is a manufactured article of any kind. If you will pile it on the shore at Montreal, Halifax, St. John, or Vancouver, and get a certified account from somebody whom we will appoint at these places, we will put you in the way of getting a cheque for your goods." Is not that a magnificent layout for the manufacturers? They do not send travelling agents abroad; they are free from that expense. They do not bother
about insuring their goods and sending them across the Atlantic; they do not worry about transportation or freight or anything else. All they have to do is produce the goods, and then this paternal fraternity known as the Government will furnish the cash and take full responsibility for everything. If that is not a scheme by which men who have goods to sell are capable of being bribed, I do not know what scheme you could devise that would be more capable of being used for bribery. I am not saying that that is what the scheme is for, but it is an old saying that the sight of means to do ill deeds, has ill deeds done. It would be better to let the men on this side of the Atlantic who have goods to sell do business direct with the men on the continent of Europe who want to buy their goods, instead of the Government engineering the thing so that the manufacturers can sell their goods for what they like without the purchaser having anything to say about it. When this matter was up about two weeks ago, the complaint was made that there was no proper distribution of these orders. Some person said there was no such thing at all as orders of this kind, but the hon. jnember for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) who, I believe, is a manufacturer or .interested in manufacturing, told us all about it. He said that the orders were distributed in the best possible way, that there was no discrimination, that everybody got a share. Nevertheless, the distribution of the orders is made by a combination of manufacturers who come together and fix their own price; they divide the orders up just as they like, and then the Government undertakes all the hard work of getting the money to pay for the goods. That is not a proper or healthy way of doing business, and the sooner we get away from it the better.
I submit that we have not been given the necessary information about this money which we are going to give to foreign countries for the purpose of stimulating trade in Canada. We do not know how much we are going to give-at least I do not; we do not know how it is to be handled; we do not know how the goods are to be bought; we do not know how they are to be conveyed from this country to their destination. When we are furnishing money in this way to help out foreigners, I submit, we should know something about it. There is all the more reason for this information because of conditions to-day, when the price

not only of foodstuffs but of manufactured articles is such that if the price were reduced to normal the sales of the manufacturers [DOT] could be doubled and trebled and our men kept at work without sending goods out of the country at all. I think that before we accept the proposition of the manufacturers, there should be the closest possible inquiry into the conditions; and the method which evidently has been adopted by the Government should only be resorted to in the last extremity when nothing else could be done to carry on trade and keep our men employed.
The information we particularly desire is in connection with the expenditure on naval affairs. We also require a little further explanation about the money we are going to borrow and pass over to foreign countries. It might be somewhat difficult for the minister to give this information to-night, but as we are entitled to it, if no other hon. member wishes to speak, I would suggest that at this late hour the minister should let the Bill stand in Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I can give my hon. friend the information that he desires to-night as to the necessity of the constitution of credits for foreign export business for Canada, and as to the manner in which that business is placed- Before doing so, however, I think I should refer to the speech of the hon. member for Lunenburg.
He covered a very wide field. I had no notice that he would bring forward the matters he dealt with to-night. It would seem to me that they would ordinarily be brought forward when the Minister of Naval Affairs had his estimates before the Committee, but the hon. member was quite in order, because we were discussing the naval estimates for the coming year as embodied in this vote. This Bill which is now before the Committee is analogous to the Bills of last year and the previous year, only that the amount is smaller and its purpose is, as hon. members know, to provide for what we might call the remainder of our war expenditure, and particularly, as the war is in reality although not officially, over, for our demobilization expenditure and other outlays arising out of the war. The Minister of Militia has explained that so far as his portion of the vote is concerned, it is solely for demobilization purposes. I would suggest to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition that as the Minister of Naval Affairs will be having his estimates before the House to-morrow or the next day,

he might deal with the statements made by the hon. member for Lunenburg on that occasion. I would submit that delay in answering the hon. member, because the minister had no notice that these matters would be brought up to-night, is not a sufficient reason for our not passing the section of the Bill referred to.
With regard to the general question of credits, let me make a rather comprehensive statement. I should like to say, first, that there is no man in the Dominion who would rather see a return to the former and normal modes of business than I. The furnishing of credits by the Dominion of Canada for the purchase of our agricultural and manufactured products is absolutely forced upon us by the exigencies of the financial situation due to the war. Take the question of our grain; I shall come to the manufactured products later. This year I had expected to have to provide a sum not exceeding $100,000,000, for the purchase of our exportable surplus of wheat and flour, but on account of the exchange situation between Great Britain and this continent by which it is impossible for Great Britain to purchase wheat in the United States and' Canada except from funds provided on this side of the Atlantic, and because no funds are available except such as we can provide in Canada, the Dominion Government has paid out up to date a sum in excess of $80,000,000, which has been loaned to the Imperial Government for the purchase ot our wheat, and it has undertaken to furnish a further $90,000,000 which will be required for the purchase of the balance of the wheat and flour products of this last year's crop. My hon. friend, I am sure, would not describe that as a bribe to the farmers. If the Dominion Government did not furnish that credit of $170,000,000-I hope it may be somewhat less, because it is a very heavy burden-then it would mean that the exportable surplus of the wheat of Canada and our exportable surplus of flour could not be bought. Under the old conditions, my hon. friend knows that the Government would not have to intervene at all, and I should be perfectly delighted if the old conditions prevailed, so that the sellers of wheat and flour would simply send forward bills of exchange with the documents attached and get their money in New York exchange. If they were able to do that there would not be to-day a 3 per cent rate of exchange against Canada as between us and the United States. So much for wheat and flour. My hon. friend would not say that we were bribing the

farmers and that we were doing, anything a government should not do at a time like this, in furnishing money which alone makes it possible for the Canadian farmer and the Canadian miller to sell their wheat and flour, and for the rest of the people of Canada to get the benefit that comes to them from the sale of those commodities.
Then as to manufactured goods. I am sure my hon. friend will not object if I ask the Committee to consider the situation with which we were confronted immediately upon the conclusion of the armistice in November last. It has often been said that preventive ability is never appreciated. People see results, but they are not aware of the cause. I have no hesitation in saying that if the Dominion Government had not faced with financial courage the situation which confronted us in November last, we should have a very grave and serious situation in Canada to-day. I believe there would have been thousands if not tens of thousands of people out of work, and I would not like to state what might have happened in Canada in consequence. If my hon. friend will go back to November last, he will realize that the entire community was greatly excited over what would happen once the war came to an end and all our war industries ceased. Directly and indirectly there were 200,000 people, men and women, engaged in munitions work and in the supply of other war material, and in other enterprises connected with those industries and in industries basic to them. That was the situation with which the Government was confronted. We had to find not only the credits with which our wheat and flour, our cheese and meat products were to be purchased, but we also had to face that very acute industrial situation which caused the utmost anxiety to the labouring population in Canada and to business generally, and to all the people interested in the welfare of the country and in the preservation of order in the community. Faced with that situation, and knowing the international financial conditions to which I have referred, the Government, at the instance of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), appointed an Overseas War Mission headed by Mr. Lloyd Harris, who did such successful work as head of the British War Mission at Washington in obtaining orders for Canada, and whose work was referred to by the President of the Privy Council in connection with his estimates the other evening. The Prime Minister went overseas himself, and accompanying him were Mr. Lloyd Harris, Mr. Frank Jones, Dr. Robertson, formerly of the Department of Agriculture, and Mr. Draper. The three important national interests, mercantile, labour, and agriculture, were represented.
Those men have been working over there most assiduously since November last, and I am surprised now to hear the hon. member for Maisonneuve ('Mr. Lemieux), although he paid the absent Minister of Trade and Commerce a compliment on the personal side, find fault with the minister whose work, to my knowledge, and on the reports which I have received from men who have been over there, ihas been of the most efficient kind for the benefit of Canada. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has really done admirable work in connection with the important question of finding markets for Canada's grain and meat products and other supplies, and the representatives of the Western Grain Growers and the Western Grain Exchange, ,who went overseas last fall, paid the highest tribute to the work done by him in connection with the important matters in which they were interested.
The Prime Minister has given the closest attention to the subject of the promotion of Canada's trade overseas. I have been in constant cable communication with him, and hundreds of cables have passed relating to matters of shipping, and to the general trade of Canada and its extension to Europe at this time. The purpose of the' Prime Minister in constituting that commission to London was to obtain business for Canada, and to take up the slack of the factory production which was interrupted by the cessation of the war. Hon. gentlemen can picture to themselves what effect the closing of these munition plants, on the scale that we had them in Canada, and of the allied industries immediately affected, would have, and what the result would be, unless we could replace that business by an equal, or at all events a large, volume of export trade. Remember we were manufacturing what we needed for ourselves and our productive capacity for munitions and war supplies bore relation to our export trade. Therefore, unless we could substitute export trade for what we had here, only one result could ensue, and that was that our industries could only run on partial capacity, and that tens of thousands of men would be out of work all over Canada. Mr, Lloyd Harris, as head of the Canadian Mission in London, has not only been doing his utmost to obtain trade for Canada, but has from the very first urged and insisted that Canadian industries

should send their own representatives over there in order that they might not only assist him, and have the benefit of the cooperation of himself and his office, but at the same time push to the utmost for business themselves; and I understand that some two hundred representatives of practically all the industries of Canada are in London to-day on the summons of Mr. Lloyd Harris, and working in co-operation with him for the benefit of our export trade. I think it is a mistake to say that that export trade is for the benefit of a few manufacturers; it seems to me .that it is not a fair statement of the situation. We often play politics in this House, but is it a fair statement to say that the promotion of the export trade of Canada is for the benefit of a few manufacturers? There are hundreds of millions of dollars-
I saw the agreement that was made for Rumania, and it seems to me it is all for the manufacturers, except one-fifth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to that in a moment. I make no objection to my hon. friend raising the question, because I am the last one to deny information on public affairs. This is an important Bill, and I desire to satisfy my hon. friend by making a very full statement: There are hundreds of millions of dollars invested [DOT] in important manufacturing establishments in this country. They employ hundreds of thousands of men whose families are maintained by their wages, and they in turn by the expenditure of their money , promote the business of the country. So that the getting of export trade for Canada for our manufactured goods, as well as for our grain and natural products, is not for the benefit of a few manufacturers, but for the welfare of the people of Canada as a whole. If, as .1 said before, we did not push for that trade, and if we did not get trade of that character for Canada, we should have a very grave situation on our hands to-day.
Now we come to the question of the credits which we shall extend. In the first place- and hon. gentlemen opposite I take it assent to that-we shall have to continue to make extensive loans to Great Britain for the purchase of our foodstuffs and the timber and other products which Great Britain will want from this country. In case some hon. gentlemen may not understand the situation, let me say that the burden on us this year is going to be very heavy because we are demobilizing in Canada, and con-

sequently. we have a higher expenditure in respect of our men coming upon the Treasury here than we would have if those men were overseas, and we were borrowing money from Great Britain for their maintenance in the Old Country and in France, and setting off that expenditure against the advances which we make to 'Great Britain here. I have explained that with respect to last year's wheat crop, we have found, or undertaken to find, no less a sum than $170,000,000, and I have no doubt that with regard to foodstuffs we shall have to make further advances to Great Britain, although I am glad to say that free markets are being established as quickly as possible with respect to all our commodities. Now we have the wheat crop of this year coming on, which we hope will be a large crop, and I do not know to what extent Europe will have to rely on us for credits for the purchase of that. But no matter what we have, we certainly must, and will, ensure the financing of the exportable surplus of the wheat crop of Canada for this year. My own view is that that should be the first demand to be satisfied, it is of such great importance to the entire country. Now we come to these other credits. There was common talk here in November of last year that Canada should strongly push for a portion of the re-construction business in Belgium, France and other devastated countries of Europe. Europe must be restored. Not only will food be required to maintain the population, but raw material and partly manufactured, and manufactured goods of various kinds, in which Canada can compete I think with any other nation, will be required on a vast scale. Now I submit that if the Government had not taken the step which it did in establishing the War Mission and providing credits, hon. gentlemen opposite, headed by my good friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) would to-night be most severely censuring the Government for not having done precisely what the Government has done. They would have very much better reason for censure in that case, because the conditions in this country, if we had not done what we did, would have been so serious that Opposition criticism would have counted very much more than it does now. Now I beg my friend the leader of the Opposition to take my word for it that we are not doing anything on the other side in the way of financing that we can avoid doing if we are to get the business.
To what other country is credit being extended besides Rumania, Belgium, and France?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Greece.

What is the amount of
credit provided by the Canadian Government to date for France and Belgium?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will make a
complete statement as to that, and I desire to say to the leader of the Opposition, and to hon. gentlemen to your left, Mr. Chairman, that I find no fault whatever with the question being raised, because an important Bill deserves serious consideration in Committee, and it is not my custom to withhold information if I can furnish it.
I desire to say to the hon. leader of the Opposition that we are in good company in what we are doing. The United States has loaned, during the war, and is loaning now, billions of dollars to the nations of Europe to enable them during the war to conduct military operations, and since to buy the products of the United States. The United States must continue to do that through her Government and her financial institutions if she is to get trade. To put it another way, if Europe is to be supplied with foodstuffs and manufactured products from this continent Europe cannot pay for them, and this continent cannot sell them unless the money is found on this side of the Atlantic. There is no business man on this side of the House who does not know that that is so. The United States has been pushing very strongly for business, as my hon. friend says, but she has been in the powerful position of being able to offer credits. Her wheat, her meats and all her other foodstuffs of every kind she can sell to Europe, but Europe cannot sell European exchange against New York exchange to pay for them; Europe has to borrow from the United States. That borrowing will he done partly from the American Government and partly by the ordinary operations between banks, and by the sale in the United States of securities of European countries.
Great Britain for many years had the greatest money market in the world in London, and foreign governments came there and sold their securities, which were taken up by British investors, and in that way the money was furnished in 'London for the purchases which were made in Great Britain. Now you have this situation on the North American continent. Our people and the people of the United States are not accustomed to buying the securities of foreign governments. The United States is
14D
very slowly becoming an international money centre because her people, until this war, had not been accustomed-as were the British people-to purchasing the securities of foreign governments. Whether they will become so accustomed to doing that as to constitute New York a great international financial centre like London, in which the securities of foreign governments will be dealt in, I do not pretend to say. It will take probably a long ' time before that is accomplished. But the United States Government has been furnishing immense sums of money to the European countries, as I have said, in order that they might purchase foodstuffs and the goods required from the United States.
I think the amount loaned to Great Britain alone is between four and five billion dollars for commodities so purchased. That was not loaned in gold and shipped overseas; it was a credit given at Washington, and Great Britain by means of that credit purchased in the United States the goods she required. She wanted the goods, and she could not buy them unless she got that credit.
With regard 'to Rumania, I would ask hon. gentlemen to bear in mind that she could have kept out of the war. She came into it at a very critical period and made great sacrifices for the common cause- 1 am not prepared to say that many thousands of Canadian lives have not been saved lby the intervention of Rumania. If hon. gentlemen will look at the map of Europe they will see that Rumania, is a; great salient projecting into Austria-Hungary, exposed to attack on both front and flank-Bulgaria to the south,. Austria-Hungary to 'the north and west. Rumania risked her all in coming into this war, and she lost for the time being, but she made the sacrifice. Sentimentally, therefore, I do not think we should be quick to reflect too much upon the credit -of Rumania, devastated as she has been by the war, prosecuted by her in common cause with the Allies. Rumania is not so strong financially, of course, as Belgium and France, but she must be restored.
