Her fields have been devastated, her cattle carried off; and her people need food and clothing and agricultural implements. How are they going to get them? If they do not get food they will starve; if they do not get clothing the consequences will be serious from exposure; if they do not get agricultural implements their tillage cannot be restored. Rumania is a very rich country, rich in her fertile plains, her splendid forests and her great oil resources, and she will get upon her



feet rapidly once she gets a chance- Now, who is going to supply to Rumania the wheat to feed her population, the clothing to protect them from the elements, and the agricultural implements and railway equipment required for the restoration of their tillage and their transportation facilities? There is an opportunity there for some nation. The United States have seized that opportunity. Since the armistice, to say nothing of before, the United States have roamed Rumania $25,000,000-I ascertained that from Washington-and all that money is being spent in the United States.
Now, our Trade Commission in London approached Belgium, France and the other nations of Europe requiring supplies of various kinds of food and for the restoration of their countries, and ascertained that there was a splendid opening for business in the Balkans, the business that I have mentioned, good for the time being to keep our factories going and afford employment to our artisans and work people, and good in its promise for the future. Rumania, as I have said, could not purchase supplies in Canada unless a credit were established; neither could France, nor Belgium; and I pointed out that even England could not purchase unless we gave her credit. We gave a credit of $25,000,000 to Rumania; we gave a credit of $25,000,000 to Greece, whose future is of the brightest; we gave a credit of $25,000,000 to Belgium, and I believe she will speedily recover from the effects of the war. Belgium is a very rich country, and is now assured of protection by the League of Nations and by the interest which Great Britain and France notably have in the preservation of its integrity.
And France?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to France, I may repeat to my hon. friend what I said the other night. The first country that we approached, long before the armistice and immediately after, in relation to reconstruction business was France. The matter was taken up with the French representative at Washington, and it was taken up overseas directly with the French Government by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Mr. Lloyd Harris, and also, I may say, by the Prime Minister; and we offered her a credit of-well, we put no limit to it. What I had in mind was a credit of from $50,000,000 to $100,000,000. No question arises of France's future. We offered her such a credit as she might require for purchases in Canada. But I

think the position of France is this, she has her own situation in regard to industries and employment, and very naturally she desires, to the extent of her ability, to do her own restoration through her own manufacturers and to give her own people employment. Consequently up to date she has not felt it necessary to avail herself of the offer of credit which I can again assure my hon. friend and this House it would have been a pleasure to us to extend to her for making purchases in this country. I have indicated all the credits that have been extended, with the exception of those which we have been giving to Great Britain and which we shall have to give. I assure the leader of the Opposition that no one will be more relieved than I shall when free markets are restored for wheat, flour, and all other commodities, so that men will carry on their business in the way they did in 1911. The hon. gentleman seemed to indicate that he thought- we were blameable because we do not do business now as we did in 1911. But he has overlooked one very important	consideration

something	for
which William Hohenzollern is responsible, not myself- and that is, the war. The reason why we have to do business in this way is that since 1911 we have had the war and we have not yet been able, as a country, to get back to the normal manner of doing business as my hon. friend described it. My own view is that as soon as industrial conditions permit, as soon as business can be done through the ordinary channels, the Dominion Government should not make any loans for the purpose of facilitating the sale of our products. The natural way is to have them taken care of through ordinary commercial and financial channels. What the Government has done it has done for two reasons: In the first place, to provide employment for those in Canada who would otherwise be out of work and to keep our factories going; and, in the second place, to extend the export trade of the country.
With regard to the -placing of orders, a point was raised the other night about commissions. I made careful inquiry of Mr. Lloyd Harris over there; he knows nothing of any commission paid in respect of the business. I also served notice upon the Trade Commission here that it was not necessary that commissions of any kind should be paid, and that no orders should be placed with firms that were paying commissions or remunerations to any outside of their own employees or organization. This business is obtained in London. The

agents of, say, 'the Rumanian Government know what they want. They deal there through the Canadian Trade Mission, and with the representatives of the various branches of Canadian manufacture. They bargain as to the prices to he paid, and they see the samples-our men are in competition with others who are competing for the same business-and then the order is placed through the Trade Commission here, which is officered by very capable and honourable men. It seems to me that we could not devise any better means of getting business for all the manufacturers of Canada than we have devised by the establishment of this Mission in London and of its complement, the Canadian Trade Mission here. It is easy to criticise, and it is hard to construct and create. But this organization which we have built up and which at the time of its inception had the commendation of the people of Canada-it was a very live question here-is to-day keeping thousands of people at work, is promoting the industry and the commerce of the country, and, 1 submit, should be commended by hon. gentlemen opposite when they get to understand it fully. At the head of our Trade Commission here is Sir Charles Gordon, a very able and honourable man, as the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) said the other night. In London we have Mr. Lloyd Harris, who is well known, I think, to most members of this House. So far as I am aware, the Government's action is such as the Government should take at a time like this. Let us look forward to a period-I do not know how far distant; I hope not far distant-when the Dominion Government will not have to provide credits; thfen we shall have the benefit of all this connection that has been established with foreign countries. Our goods will get to be known, and an impetus will be given to all the industry of the country.
As to indebtedness on the part of one Government to another, that is usually a very honourable obligation of Governments and I have no doubt whatever that the advances which are being made by the Dominion Government, substantial sums as they are, will be repaid in due course, as soon as peace conditions permit these nations again to get upon their feet, and as soon as international exchange is restored.
What is the rate of interest charged ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We could have charged six, six and-a-half or seven per
1404	i
cent, but we are dealing with Governments and we did not think that it was dignified to charge an extortionate rate of interest. We charge them just the rate it costs to raise the money here-five and one-half per cent.
Most of these European countries are protective countries. Will the goods be subject to customs duties when they reach these countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say as to that; but these goods are being purchased by Governments, and Governments could no doubt arrange to have them go in free of duty. Our relationship is not with individuals in these countries, but with Governments. For example, we give the Belgium Government a credit of $25,000,000, and Belgium is going to send a mission out here to purchase. The Belgian Government, having borrowed the money from us, and being, as I believe, entirely responsible, will use its credit in this country to purchase to the best advantage. I think the Hudson's Bay Company has been doing some buying for the Belgian Government. I believe that Greece also will send a mission here to purchase. Of the Rumanian credit, $5,000,000 is in wheat, another $5,000000 is in raw material-that has not yet been purchased-and the ' balance is in manufactured products, such as clothing, woollens, textiles, agricultural implements, and, I hope, some railway equipment; in other words, what they need in order to restore their country.
Hon. gentlemen may say that Canada is taking some risk in this matter. Well, let us assume that we are. Having regard to the situation in which the country found itself in November last, facing this collapse in its industries, Canada is abundantly justified in doing what the United States has been doing on an immense scale, and what Great Britain is doing. This war has caused so profound a dislocation in the world, in finance, commerce and industry, that if during this year, which, in a sense, is a war year, because we have the consequences of the war with us, we failed in courage or in resource, the situation would be different in Canada from what it is to-day. I do not believe hon. gentlemen, no matter how well informed they may be, quite appreciate what 'the Government's financing has done and is doing for this country to-day. If you take the gratuity which we gave the soldiers; if you take the payments to the soldiers that the Minister of Militia has referred

to; if you take our shipbuilding programme; if you take the immense expenditures we are obliged to make for the financing of our grain purchases and our manufactured products that I have mentioned- hundreds of dollars-and then imagine the situation if the Government on November 11 had said:	"Now we quit right here;
the war is at an end; no more credits for wheat or meats or manufactured products; let private enterprise carry on the business itself. Well, I would be taking a ticket out of the country, because I would not desire to face the situation which would have resulted. Imagine the activities of this country, stimulated as they were during .the war, keyed up to a height that none of us believed they could attain, and then everything suddenly stop. If the Government had not come to the rescue as they did, with courage and resource, and provide the credits we did, there would have been a very serious situation in Canada.
Does the minister include transportation charges in the credit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of the $25,000,000 mentioned, there is a sum of $1,000,000, I think, for transportation. If my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) desires that this Bill should be taken up again to-morrow afternoon or evening, I have so much respect for his request that I will agree to it, and I do not think it will take very long to finish with the Bill- As regards the observations of the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who was Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries, may make a brief statement, but I will direct the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne) to them in order that he may take them up when his Estimates are under consideration. This is a general Bill; it follows the lines of the previous Bills, both as to drafting and otherwise, and it is for demobilization as the others were for war; and it seems that the matters referred to to-night, especially those referred to by the hon. member for Lunenburg, might very well be taken up on the Estimates.

There is no doubt the matters discussed by the hon. member for Lunenburg could be discussed on the Estimates; but I think when the Acting Prime Minister considers that he has himself admitted that the hon. member is quite in order in bringing them up on this Bill, it is on this Bill that the answer should be made, because when the minister comes along CSir Thomas White.]
with his Estimates, it will then be necessary for the hon. member to make his speech over again and put those facts before the minister in connection with another matter. We want to avoid that and to save time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is going into Estimates to-morrow afternoon and intends to make a statement on shipbuilding and to take up items on his Estimates. The minister will then be able to deal with the observations of the hon. member for Lunenburg and the passing of this Bill need not be delayed because of the observations of the hon. member. On Supply or on any money Bill, it is proper for grievances of any kind ,to be brought forward; it is not necessary that they should be answered unless they seem to be relevant in some way to the vote, but I am quite sure the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will be glad to speak to the observations of the hon. member for Lunenburg, and in the meantime, while I should like to get this Bill through, it ,can stand until to-morrow afternoon when ,we can take it up, and, I have no doubt, finish it quickly.

The minister was kind enough to direct his observations very largely to myself. He has not in any way cleared his Government from the responsibility of starting this new venture of opening credits in a foreign country with .which we never did any business before. We have done our share in connection with the war nobly and well, particularly as an ally of our Mother Country, and nobody is finding very much fault with any moneys that have been expended in that direction. But I say to the Acting Prime Minister that we are under no obligation to build up Rumania or any other country that might have of its own free will gone into the war and received some damage by reason of that fact. It is going too far to ask the Canadian people, who have not the money ,to spend, who have to borrow money for their own purposes, who cannot, by reason of the high cost of living and other matters, get all the money they require for their own purposes, to furnish this money; and the Acting Prime Minister is going too far in looking for sympathy and applause from his supporters to-night by saying that we are doing this in the generosity of our hearts and extreme loyalty in order to build up the finances df Rumania, because that country got into trouble with its neighbours and not because- of any loyalty to us.

I have no fault to find with advancing credits to Great Britain, France, Italy or Belgium because, if the Acting Prime Minister had the securities of those
12 p.m countries in his vault, he could easily raise money on them from	any	hank in this countryor in the United States. But the trade	that	we	went	after,	by and
through our Trade Mission, was the trade of a country whose securities are evidently not very good in this country, upon which securities the Acting Prime Minister cannot raise any money and which, as the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) stated, are being peddled about from bucket shop to bucket shop in London at much below par- What we should have done is to deal with Great Britain and France, and if Great Britain and France want to advance goods to those smaller powers who are under their control and who must pay for them or get into trouble, that would be good business. We could very well say to the British Government: We will give you all the credit you want; we will arrange that we send the goods to you, and you can deal with the smaller countries. We never had any dealings with those countries in the most prosperous days of Canada, and why should we now pass over the heads of France, Italy and Great Britain and seek trade with countries with which we have never dealt with before? That is the particular fault I have to find. It is stated that our Trade Mission and our Trade Ministers were so clumsy and slow and incompetent in securing trade that everything that was worth having was gone and they were glad enough at last to fall back on such trade as they could make with Rumania by offering Rumania the money. That is where the difficulty is. If our manufacturers were properly represented on the other side by live business men, they would have secured the orders that the United States manufacturers got, but we did not get them, and our representatives, in order to do something to justify their existence on the other side, had to make this masterful stroke of saying to Rumania: We will give you money if you will be kind enough to buy our goods. That is all they did for which they claim so much credit, and I do not think they have shown any great foresight or capacity because they have done that.
I want to be absolutely fair to the manufacturers. We have manufacturers in the part of the country from which I come, manufacturing rails and all kinds of structural steel. They got no help from the Government.
Will.the hon. member say what means were taken to provide the Steel Company at Sydney with orders .so that they could continue manufacturing steel rails?

The Minister of Railways found it proper, with a view to building three or four, or ten, thousand miles of railway next summer, to secure contracts for rails at a price below war prices. That is all that was done, and I am quite satisfied that any such a contract should be made with any manufacturer in the *country. The Nova Scotia Steel had to *send out their own agent to London and do the best they could to make contracts for themselves. Colonel Can'tley went to London representing the Nova Scotia Steel. The company got no help from any body. Some of their men had to be laid off for ,a couple of months because there was not enough work to keep things going; but they had good times during the war and they had to put up with the difficulties that came their way, without any help from the Government. If the Nova Scotia Steel and other concerns in the part of Canada from which I come have to forage for themselves and find a market for their product as best they can, I cannot understand why other concerns should not do the same thing.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that Colonel Cantley was unable to get any contracts in England because of the difficulty of financing over there?

I am not aware of any such difficulty. I am aware that while the men were idle for a while, they have now gone back to work and everything is going on first-class. The company did not get a cent of assistance from this Government or anybody else.

Colonel Cantley was
not able to get any contracts overseas.

I am not saying whether he was or not. I know he went over there to try and get contracts. I know that the steel works are now working on their own initiative without a dollar of assistance from this Government, and what they have done other concerns should be able to do. But no one will exert himself if the Minister of Finance is going to take the whole responsibility on himself and relieve him of all his difficulties. I am sure the Nova

Scotia Steel and the Dominion Iron & Coal and other concerns in Nova Scotia would he delighted to jump at such an opportunity as that, but they had to get along by themselves, and they got along fairly well, and I think that is a more healthy way of doing business in any country. I would suggest that at this late hour the Bill should stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will take it up to-morrow.

When the resolution on which-this Bill is founded was before the House I asked the Minister of Finance when the Order in Council had been passed with reference to the Rumanian loan, -and he promised to give me the information. I already knew that an Order in Council had been passed, but the Prime Minister promised to get that information. A fortnight or three weeks have passed and the information has not yet been brought down as to when that Order in Council was passed granting a credit to Rumania. I understand it was passed only four or five days before the resolution was discussed in the House, but I should like to know the exact .date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I paid so much attention to the request of my hon. friend that I laid the Order in Council on the Table the next day. The Order in Council was passed as soon as the agreement signed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister of Rumania came to hand. It could not be passed before that agreement had come to hand. I would not like my hon. friend to think I was guilty of any discourtesy.

The minister must have laid it on the Table sotto voce. It is strange that the Government should pass an Order in Council granting a credit to Rumania when the people's representatives were assembled here in Parliament, and I wish to protest against any such action of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The assistant clerk calls my attention to the fact that on the 11th of April, as I stated, I laid the Order in Council on the Table.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh with great glee because the Order in Council was laid on the Table without the knowledge of a private member. I wish to say with .reference to laying Orders in Council on the Table, that that is no proper means of communicating information to

this House. I have complained about it dozens of times. Whenever an important Order in Council or .any important document is to be laid on the Table, a copy of it should be put in the box of every hon. member. We cannot hear a word in this House; I can hardly hear a word myself, and it is much worse for hon. gentlemen sitting behind. An Order in Council can be laid on the Table without any one being the wiser. We cannot always be standing over the clerk to see what is being laid on the Table. I repeat, when any information is laid on the Table of which hon. members should be made aware, a copy should be placed in every member's box, just as is done with the Estimates.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Sir Thomas White, the House adjourned at 12.15 a.m., Thursday.
